Explanatory Introduction: The Fivefold Profundity (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*) was unfolded by Fazang (*Xianshou*), who expounded the sutras by opening ten gates of wondrous intent. Now, as I compose this text, I have merely provided a brief commentary on the title of the sutra and have not opened with a prolegomenon (*xuantan*). Why is this so? Answer: One who masters the principles of integrity and excels in adaptability propagates the teaching through the person. For instance, when Guishan annotated the *Sutra of Forty-two Sections*, how could there have been a "Profound Meaning" (*xuan-yi*) section? It is simply that the circumstances differ. Thus, while the *Avataṃsaka* is vast and profound, the *Forty-two Sections* is concise and direct; the former requires extensive exposition, whereas the latter does not. This is the reason for my approach. Furthermore, the *Forty-two Sections* is a small scripture, and its meaning is already clear within the text itself; therefore, I have not elaborated further. Moreover, the *Forty-two Sections* is a work of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), whereas the *Avataṃsaka* is the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*). Since the two vehicles differ in their depth and breadth, it would be inappropriate to apply the same methods of explanation. For these reasons, I have omitted the prolegomenon. Finally, the *Forty-two Sections* is a foundational text for beginners, and its purpose is to provide a general introduction to the Dharma. If one were to add a prolegomenon, it would become overly complex and fail to serve its function as an introductory guide.

Therefore, I have followed this principle. I hope that those who read this will understand my intention. If there are any errors or omissions, I beg for your correction. I shall now proceed to explain the title of the sutra. [End of Explanatory Introduction] *Sutra of the Buddha’s First Turning of the Wheel of the Dharma* (佛說轉法輪經) **Commentary on the Title:** First, regarding "The Buddha" (*Buddha*): This refers to the World-Honored One (*bhagavān*). He is called "Buddha" because he has awakened to the true nature of all phenomena, having severed ignorance and attained perfect enlightenment.

He is called "World-Honored One" because he possesses the six supreme qualities and is honored by all worlds. Second, regarding "Said" (*śāsita*): This means that the sutra was spoken by the Buddha. It indicates that the words and meanings herein are the authentic teachings of the Tathāgata, not the compositions of humans or devas. Third, regarding "Turning the Wheel of the Dharma" (*dharmacakra-pravartana*): "Dharma" refers to the True Dharma (*saddharma*), which is the path of liberation. "Wheel" (*cakra*) signifies movement and pervasiveness; it represents the power of the Dharma to turn and transform sentient beings. "Turning" (*pravartana*) means to set in motion. This refers to the Buddha’s first sermon at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī, where he turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths for the five bhikṣus, thereby establishing the foundation of the Buddhist teachings. Fourth, regarding "Sutra" (*sūtra*): This is the name of the genre. It means "to string together" (*sīv-*) or "to summarize. It refers to the collection of the Buddha’s teachings, which string together the various meanings like beads on a thread. Thus, the full title means: The sutra spoken by the Buddha concerning the turning of the wheel of the Dharma. [End of Commentary on the Title]

"I heard. This refers to the accomplishment of hearing. "I" refers to Ānanda, a provisional designation for the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). "Hearing" refers to the faculty of the ear (*śrotrendriya*), which gives rise to consciousness to perceive and receive [the object].

"At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) refers to the perfection of time. Because the teacher and disciples have assembled and the teaching and listening have reached their conclusion, it is said "at one time.
Since the divisions of time differ across various regions—being either extended or abbreviated—it is simply stated as "one."

"Buddha" means the "Master of Accomplishment. In full, it is called *Buddha*, which translates as "The Awakened One. This refers to one who has awakened to and understood both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, it possesses three meanings:

Having eliminated all discrimination, he has attained liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*); having forever eradicated what is co-nascent (*sahaja*), he has attained liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*). This is likewise equal to the Great [Vehicle].

By means of this vehicle, one severs the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and attains liberation of mind (*cittavimukti*); one severs the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and attains liberation through wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*).
Both of these clarify the two liberations of mind and wisdom in terms of severing the two types of delusions—the coarse and the subtle.
The traditional interpretation states that among Arhats, those of sharp faculties are called "liberated in mind," while those of dull faculties are called "liberated through wisdom."
The nine knowledges and ten knowledges have accomplished what was to be done.

The nine knowledges eliminate the coarse [afflictions] of discrimination; the ten knowledges eliminate the subtle [afflictions] that are innate. Since these two types of delusion have perished, what was to be done has been accomplished.

The nine knowledges are: conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), and knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).

Knowledge consists of: knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

Regarding these ten knowledges, the traditional interpretation holds that those of dull faculties who have attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) possess the first nine knowledges, whereas Arhats of sharp faculties possess the final knowledge of non-arising as well.

One may seek it through emptiness; do not weary of elaborate texts. △ Fourth, regarding the preaching of the Dharma by all Buddhas:
therein, each and every Buddha proclaims the *prajñāpāramitā*, which spreads and circulates throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Among them, the "various Buddhas" refers back to the previously mentioned transformation Buddhas. △ Third, the description of the assembly taking their seats:
All these various members of the great assembly who had come forth each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.

This single recitation of the sutra summarizes both assemblies. If one were to conclude [the assembly] solely by binding the supporting retinue without including those who are the primary recipients of the teaching, this would achieve the immediate while losing the ultimate.
△ Second, the Prologue of the Arousing of the Teaching. Now, as for the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*:
The *Lotus Sūtra* merely manifests entering meditative concentration, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* simply clarifies the emission of light;

how could they compare to the present sūtra, which first enters dhyāna and subsequently emits radiance, thereby using the essence to support the function and giving rise to the true teaching of Prajñā? This text consists of five sections.
At the time when he first manifested the teaching of the Dharma,
the World-Honored One was endowed with immeasurable virtues and was revered by the world.

The first day of the eighth month of the year refers to the initial year of the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Regarding the eighth day of the first month, Qingliang (Kuiji) cites the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha as saying:
"Seven years prior, he taught the Four Noble Truths, which was called 'Turning the Wheel of Dharma. Seven years later, he taught the *Prajñāpāramitā*. This completes [the account].

It turns its light upon the two wheels; because it illuminates existence by means of emptiness. Since it is stated that the *Prajñāpāramitā* will be preached after seven years, this must refer to the beginning of the eighth year.
Some may ask: "According to the subsequent text, the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā* are at the beginning, while this sutra is situated later.
What is the intent of this? The answer is: Teachings have both fundamental and manifest aspects, and times have their sequence of priority and posteriority. As for their...

Fundamentally, a single sound is manifested all at once, yet each according to its kind understands it differently. To speak of its traces, this was the first teaching for the eight classes of beings, while this sutra was expounded later.
If one can reach the root and forget the traces, then the wondrous chanting of the single sound will be realized;
if one does not cling to the sequence of before and after, then the profound purport of Prajñāpāramitā may perhaps be found therein. △ Second, entering meditative concentration.
He emits light and enters the sublime samādhi of great tranquility.

"Entering" means that the mind and its object merge into one; "sublime" means that the path of discursive thought is severed; and "great tranquility" refers to the ultimate state of meditative concentration.
*Samādhi* is translated as "wisdom" (*hui*). It refers to the simultaneous flow of stillness and illumination.
According to the *Śrī-laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-vyākhyā*, *samāpatti* is here translated as "contemplation" (*guan*), based on its application to causal practice.
From all the pores of his body, he emitted great radiance that universally illuminated Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
The body hairs represent the primary retribution (*pratyaya-phala*), while the Buddha-lands represent the secondary retribution (*āśraya-phala*).

Since his entry into meditative concentration was already a simultaneous flow of quiescence and illumination, the emission of light constituted the mutual penetration of the secondary and primary retributions. △ Third, the devas rained down flowers.
At that time, the immeasurable devas of the desire realm rained down a multitude of exquisite flowers;
"multitude" refers to their many different colors, while "exquisite" refers to how they universally gladden all receptive capacities.
The devas of the form realm likewise rained down celestial flowers, with various colors intermingled, which were exceedingly lovely and delightful.

Their branches spread and hang down, with various colors reflecting one another; thus they are called "intermingled. The varieties of flowers are exquisite and peerless; beholding them in stillness never leads to weariness;
thus they are termed "delightful."
At that time, in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), various fragrant flowers rained down.

Through the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) arising from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the fragrant flowers spread everywhere. The upper part presents the two headings; the lower part provides the two explanations.
The fragrance was like Mount Sumeru, and the flowers were like chariot wheels.
Rising up in swirling clouds, it was both wondrous and lofty, like Mount Sumeru; its fragrance pervaded the void, circling and revolving again and again, like a chariot wheel.

Thus, while the devas of the Desire Realm merely rained down exquisite flowers, those of the Form Realm interspersed them with various blossoms to create a delightful spectacle, and the devas of the Formless Realm let fall both incense and flowers together.
This, too, reflects the differences in the ascent and descent across the various realms and stages.
This causes the fragrant flowers to appear extraordinary. The upper part lists them individually; the lower part refers to them collectively.
They descend like clouds, covering the entire assembly.
Although non-material sentient beings lack the form resulting from karma, they possess the form resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi*); therefore, fragrance rains down.
It resembles a mountain. Scattered flowers form circles like wheels. △ Fourth, shaking the earth to alert the assembly:
throughout the entire Buddha-world, there are six kinds of tremors.
"Shaking" (zhèn) refers to sound; "moving" (dòng) refers to form. Sound includes roaring and striking; form includes rising and surging. Therefore, there are six.
These six each have three aspects, forming eighteen characteristics, as detailed in the *Huayan jing shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra).
In the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, seven causes are taught: first, to cause all Māras to give rise to alarm and fear; second, to prevent the minds of the assembly from being distracted;
third, to cause those who are heedless to attain awakening; fourth, to cause sentient beings to keep the Dharma in mind.
5. Because it causes sentient beings to contemplate the locus of the teaching; 6. because it enables those who are mature to attain liberation; 7.
because it allows them to inquire in accordance with the true meaning. △ Fifth: Raising Doubts to Manifest the Dharma (six points). First: Narrating past doubts regarding the present.
At that time, the great assembly said to one another: "The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One has previously expounded for us the Mahāprajñāpāramitā,
the Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā, the Prajñāpāramitā asked by the Heavenly Kings,
the Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā, and countless, immeasurable prajñāpāramitās such as these."
The Prajñāpāramitā consists of eight sections, yet the sūtra text lists only three;
hence the word "etcetera" (ādi), which includes the *Svalpikā*, *Mārgajñatā*, *Prabhāsa*, *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, and the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā*.
Today the Tathāgata has emitted a great radiance. What deed does this portend?
△ Second, King Prasenajit poses his inquiry. Part four: First, reflecting on the Dharma and its benefit to sentient beings.
At that time, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit of the Bārāṇasī thought to himself: "Now the Buddha has manifested this rare phenomenon..."
Signs: it will surely rain the Dharma-rain, universally benefiting all.
Śrāvastī is translated here as "Abundant Virtue," meaning it is fully endowed with wealth, treasures, sensory objects, extensive learning, liberation, and so forth.
This refers to the capital city of the Kosalā kingdom in India. According to the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), there were two Kosala kingdoms, one in the north and one in the south.
To distinguish it from the southern kingdom, both the city and the kingdom are mentioned here. △ Second, the question of the assembly and the statement of doubt.
He then questioned the lay followers, such as Ratnacchattra and Vimalakīrti;
these were members of the householders' assembly. The elder Ratnākara was so named because he offered a parasol to the Buddha.
Vimalakīrti is the lay devotee (upāsaka) known as Pure Name.
Śāriputra, Subhūti, and others were the great śrāvakas, the assembly of the Hīnayāna.
Śāriputra is called "Son of the Śāris" (Qiuzi) in this land; Subhūti is translated here as "Good Appearance" (Shanxian).
"Maitreya, Siṃhanāda," and so forth—these refer to the assembly of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of the Mahāyāna.
"Maitreya" is translated here as "The Benevolent One" (Cishi). "Siṃhanāda" (Lion's Roar) refers to preaching the Dharma within the assembly while having attained great fearlessness.
The former [section] consists of the questions posed by the assembly; the latter describes the doubts [of the listeners].
It was asked: "What auspicious sign is this manifested by the Tathāgata?
King Prasenajit, a Great Being of the Dharma-body, having witnessed the manifestation of this omen, knew that the Eightfold Supreme Proclamation would surely be proclaimed;
it was from this that [the assembly] was inspired. △ Third, none among the multitude offered a reply.
At that time, none among the great assembly were able to answer.

The Buddha’s wisdom was profound and deep; because it transcended human reach, it could not be fathomed. This demonstrated that what he taught must have reached the most subtle and mysterious depths. △ Fourth:
Offering Music to the Buddha.
King Prasenajit and others, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, performed music on a vast scale.
The various devas of the realms of desire and form each played countless celestial instruments, the sound of which pervaded the trichiliocosm.
He questioned [them], but there was no answer. It would not do to remain idle; thus, music was played as an offering to the Buddha while awaiting the sound of the Dharma.
△ Third, emitting light to summon the assembly:
At that time, the World-Honored One again emitted immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya rays of light, their brilliance a mixture of various colors.
The previous emission of light did not specify its number, signifying the realization of principle through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

This present emission of light, however, specifies "immeasurable variegated colors," signifying the teaching of the Dharma and the salvation of beings through subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). △ Fourth, the proclamation of the teaching within the light.

Within each and every ray of light, there appear precious lotus flowers; each flower has a thousand petals, all of which are golden in color. Upon them are transformation Buddhas, proclaiming the essential points of the Dharma.

The light manifests lotus flowers, all of which are golden in color, signifying that their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is unstained. The Buddha’s preaching of the essential Dharma signifies the inclusion of the dharmas of fruition.

Furthermore, the manifestation of lotus flowers within the light signifies the dharma of practice (*pratipatti-dharma*); their being golden in color signifies the dharma of principle (*naya-dharma*). The transformation Buddhas upon them signify the dharma of fruition;
the proclamation of the essential Dharma signifies the dharma of teaching (*deśanā-dharma*). However, in this present sutra, the teaching is proclaimed within the light itself.
Regarding the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and the "Emission of Light" (Ratnarāśi-parivarta) where the mantra is spoken: if one examines their wording, they differ slightly;

yet if one investigates their essential meaning, they are largely the same. Why is this? That sutra states: "At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness.

This is identical to the present text which says: "At that time, the World-Honored One again emitted immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya rays of light. Furthermore, regarding what that sutra says about "within the light":
A thousand-petaled precious lotus emerges; within each of these individual rays of light, precious lotuses appear, each with a thousand petals.
It is said that there, a transformation body of the Buddha sits in the full lotus posture and proclaims a divine mantra;

this refers to the transformation Buddhas above who proclaim the essentials of the Dharma. Furthermore, the dharma-gates thus symbolized are all contained within the introductory section on the arousal of the aspiration.

[End of section] Now, although these two sutras present their sublime teachings with a sequence of priority and posteriority, when one synthesizes their essential tenets, they are truly what is called "different paths leading to the same destination.
△ Five: The Universal Gathering of Those with Karmic Connections (3). First: General Statement.

This is the light of the Buddha. Throughout the lands of the Buddhas in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it manifests wherever there are those with whom he has a karmic affinity.
Thus, the path of response and the path of invocation meet, and the opportune moment is never missed. △ Second, the detailed enumeration.
In those Buddha-lands of other directions, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabha in the east emits light that shines everywhere,
making no distinction between enemies and kin;
and in the southeast, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Padmapāṇi.
His myriad practices are untainted, universally responding to the capacities of all beings.
To the south is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Free from Sorrow;
there are no obstacles he has not exhausted, and his name "Free from Sorrow" accords with reality.
In the southwest is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Radiant Light;
his wisdom-light shines within, and his bodily light illuminates without.
In the west is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Practice-Wisdom.
In all practices he performs, he takes wisdom as his light.
To the northwest is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnavijaya,
whose mind is adorned with the jewel of wisdom, surpassing all ordinary beings and śrāvakas.
In the north is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Viśeṣābhyudgata, who,
having fully perfected all supreme virtues, has received the rank of Dharma King.
In the northeast is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaprabha.
Wisdom realizes suchness, free from all defilements and obstructions.
Above, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Joyful Reception instructs sentient beings, and they joyfully receive it.
From below, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Padmavijaya,
whose nature is unstained and who surpasses all fragrant flowers,
arrived here together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas.
*Koṭi* means "ten million" according to the translation by the Tang Tripiṭaka Master. △ Sixth, making offerings and paying homage:
Holding various incenses, scattering various flowers, and performing immeasurable music, they made offerings to the Tathāgata, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit silently.
"To remain silent" means to wish and desire to hear. The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* says:
"Like one who thirsts longs for cool water, like one who is hungry thinks of fine food, like one who is ill remembers an excellent medicine, or like a bee covets sweet honey—so too are we."
"I pray to hear the Dharma of the Deathless.
With palms joined in reverence, he single-mindedly contemplated the Buddha.
In the preceding *samyak-saṃpratyaya-nidāna* (序), it merely states that "each paid homage at the Buddha's feet and withdrew to sit on one side"; now, in the *samutthāna-nidāna* (發起序), it further...
Regarding the phrase "joining palms with reverence and contemplating the Buddha with a single mind," this refers to the initiation of the main teaching (*samyak-artha*), which has two aspects:
first, the title of the chapter, namely the "Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata"; second, the scriptural text itself, namely "contemplating the true mark of the body;
contemplating the Buddha is likewise. From here below, six chapters clarify the section of the main teaching. The first three chapters clarify the internal [practice].
[The section on] Protection. The final three chapters clarify external protection. Now, regarding the first [section], the protection of the fruit, there is a brief opening in three gates.

In the second chapter, "Contemplating the Tathāgata," there are two intentions for its inclusion: first, its sequence within the division; second, its sequence within the chapter. Regarding the first, within the three divisions, from here below is the main body.

The Thesis: Since the causal conditions have already been clarified, the primary teaching (*mauladharmatā*) ought now to be revealed; therefore, the next section follows. Regarding the arrival of these two chapters, there are two meanings:

first, whereas the preceding section distinguished the assembly of followers, the present one reveals the Teacher; second, whereas previously the causes for the person were established, the present one fully details the protection of the fruit;
thus, the next section follows. Second, regarding the explanation of the title: wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*) is the subject that contemplates, and the Tathāgata is the object contemplated.
The title is established by designating both the subject and the object. For instance, the single epithet "Tathāgata" possesses five meanings:

first, it is explained in terms of principle (*li*), wherein "thusness" (*tathatā*) refers to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and "coming" (*āgata*) refers to emerging from obstructions. Second, it is explained solely in terms of practice (*xing*);

as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because his words are not false, he is called Tathāgata. Third, it is explained through the union of wisdom and principle; as the *Dharmacakra-pravartana-śāstra* states: "First... [text continues].
"Truth" (*tathā*) means "suchness. "Come" (*āgata*) means "perfectly awakened. This is explained through four aspects of detachment from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-viveka*):

the *Prajñāpāramitā* states that because there is nowhere from which he comes and nowhere to which he goes, he is called the Tathāgata. This is explained through five aspects of integration (*yuganaddha*): it means that the suchness of one is the suchness of two;

whether in principle (*li*) or wisdom (*jñāna*), whether opened or closed, everything is without exception suchness. Therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. There is no dharma outside of suchness; he has come [from this].
This is also "Thusness. One who comes in this manner is a true Tathāgata. △ Third, the explanation of the scripture, which contains seven parts.
First, the Tathāgata arises from meditative absorption and grants permission to speak. Second, first, he prefaces the request by acknowledging the thoughts of the various kings.
At that time,
when the assembly had gathered,
the World-Honored One arose from samādhi.
In the Sanskrit language, *samādhi* is translated here as "equipoise" (*samāhita*).
Seated upon the lion throne, he addressed the great assembly, saying: "I know that the sixteen kings and their retinues have all conceived this thought."
The World-Honored One possesses great compassion and universally brings benefit and joy to all. How, then, should we kings protect our nations?

Through the internal illumination of true wisdom and the external clarity of expedient wisdom, it is known that the kings have brought forth their thoughts to request protection for their nations. II.
Granting the Teaching on Internal Protection and Admonishing the Audience to Listen.
"Good son, this is the designation for one who acts with firm resolve in accordance with principle.
I shall now first explain for all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas the protection of the fruit of Buddhahood and the protection of the practices of the ten stages."
The King requested protection for the state. As for why he first explained the causes and effects of protection, there are two intentions:
first, it is because if one wishes to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed, nothing is better than a thorough entrustment; thus, he first [taught] for the sake of the Bodhisattvas.
Second, it is because if there were no internal protection through causes and effects, external calamities would have no way to be completely extinguished.
All of you should listen attentively, listen attentively. Contemplate it well. I exhort you to be thorough and discerning;
do not use a mind characterized by arising and ceasing to hear the Dharma of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Through attentive listening, one gains the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);

through careful contemplation, the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and through mindfulness, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). If these three wisdoms serve as the cause, one will certainly realize [enlightenment].
The fruit of the five patiences. △ Second, King Prasenajit rejoices and scatters flowers.
At that time, the great assembly, including King Prasenajit and others, having heard the Buddha’s words, all praised him together, saying: “Excellent, excellent!”

Regarding the repeated exclamation "Excellent!": The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that this is the ultimate expression of goodness. By means of the two protections of cause and effect, one upholds the essentials of the Buddha-dharma;
internally, one causes the Three Jewels to flourish, and externally, one dispels the seven calamities. Having been granted permission to speak, the benefit and joy are truly manifold;
thus, the great assembly rejoices and praises it repeatedly.
Immediately, immeasurable and wondrous jewel flowers were scattered, which transformed in mid-air into a jeweled canopy that covered the entire assembly,
pervading everywhere without exception.
If this represents a Dharma-gate, then the transformation into a jeweled canopy in mid-air signifies the functioning within the single void.
It covered the entire assembly, pervading everywhere without exception, becoming silent within the realm of the ten thousand transformations.
△ Third, inquiring into the profound meaning of cause and effect.
At that time, King Prasenajit rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms, knelt on both knees, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva protect the fruit of buddhahood? How does he protect the practices of the ten stages?”
"Rising from one's seat" means rising when requested to teach and rising when beginning a new topic. Now, asking about the two types of protection (*rakṣā*) constitutes the beginning of a new topic.
△ Fourth, the extensive answer concerning the gate of contemplating the fruits of protection has two parts. First, transforming sentient beings of the four modes of birth has three sections.
First, the result is set forth by taking the four modes of birth as its object.
The Buddha told King Prasenajit: "Those who would protect the fruit of Buddhahood—the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—should abide in this manner."
Ultimate wisdom illuminates the truth and does not abide in existence; expedient wisdom penetrates the conventional and does not abide in emptiness.
With the unimpeded integration of the expedient and the ultimate, one achieves the practice of non-abiding and teaches and transforms all beings born from eggs, wombs, moisture, and transformation.
To transform and guide all four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) is compassion (*karuṇā*). That, in reality, there are no four modes of birth to be transformed is wisdom (*prajñā*).

Regarding the explanation of the meaning of the four modes of birth, there are three distinctions: the mode of birth, the basis, and the objective sphere (*viṣaya*), as explained in the two commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Vajracchedikā*.
△ Second, cultivating the causes by taking the two practices as the object of contemplation, in two parts. First, a brief explanation based on the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
One does not contemplate the characteristics of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), nor does one contemplate the suchness of form (*rūpa-tathatā*).
Because of possessing wisdom, one realizes that form is itself true emptiness; thus, one does not contemplate its characteristics.
Because of possessing compassion, one penetrates that form is illusory existence; thus, one does not contemplate its suchness. △ Second, extending this to other dharmas for a broad analysis.
Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness:

the inversions of self, person, knower, and viewer, as well as permanence, pleasure, and purity, are first illustrated by analogy with the other four aggregates, and subsequently the four inversions are clarified. Now, concerning the statement that the inversion of "self" refers to the "knower and viewer":

this means that based upon the aggregates, one falsely clings [to them]. Thus, there is the false clinging to a person, as well as false knowing and false viewing. If one applies the method of contemplation to illustrate this, it is explained as follows.

It is compassion within wisdom; one does not observe the characteristics of sensation (*vedanā*). It is wisdom within compassion; one does not observe the suchness (*tathatā*) of sensation. The remaining seven [objects] are to be understood by analogy with this.
The above illustrates defiled objects; the following illustrates pure objects.
The four means of integration and the six perfections; the two truths and the four truths;
likewise, through the two practices of compassion and wisdom, one does not perceive characteristics or suchness, nor the powers, the fearlessnesses, or any other such dharmas.
The ten powers and four fearlessnesses, as well as the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), are all practices within the causal stage.
This applies likewise to both bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas; they do not contemplate marks (*lakṣaṇa*), nor do they contemplate suchness (*tathatā*).

Beginning from sensation and perception and ending with the Tathāgata, all are characterized by the two practices of compassion and wisdom. Because they do not perceive [these states] as having fixed characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is stated in general terms:
"It is also thus. △ Third, the investigation and explanation of "perceiving characteristics as such" (*lakṣaṇa-samāna*) to conclude the contemplation of the mind, in three parts:
first, the dual inquiry.
Why is this so? Why is it that one does not contemplate the marks as being such? △ Second, the dual explanation:
because the nature of all phenomena is itself reality.
Because the nature of all phenomena is the very substance of true emptiness, there is no coming and no going, and no arising and no ceasing.
Since its essence is utterly beyond delusion and awakening, there is no coming or going; since its nature is neither defiled nor pure, there is no arising or ceasing.
They share the same reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) and are equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); they are non-dual and without distinction, just like empty space.

Since there is one suchness and no second suchness, it is said that they are without distinction. Empty space has two meanings: first, the sense of being all-pervasive, which is identical to the reality-limit;
second, the sense of containing and encompassing, which is equal to the nature of all phenomena. The above explains how compassion exists without observing [suchness]. Below—
The commentary states: One who possesses wisdom does not contemplate characteristics.
Regarding the characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), there is neither self nor what belongs to a self.
By examining the three categories one by one, it is seen that there is not only no self, but also nothing belonging to a self. △ Third, the summary.
This is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
△ Second, the demonstration of the three kinds of *prajñā*. Master Xianshou said: First is the *dharmatā* (real mark), which refers to the true nature that is the object of contemplation;

second is the *pratyavekṣaṇā* (contemplative illumination), which refers to the wondrous wisdom that is the subject of contemplation; third is the *vyañjana* (words/letters), which refers to the teachings that express the former two. Now, according to this...
This section of the sutra implicitly sets forth its fundamental tenets. The text has two parts. First, from the root arises the branches, explained in accordance with the sequence.

Within this, first, the true nature that is the object of contemplation is clarified through the real mark (*dharmatā*). This has three parts. First, the question regarding the contradiction between the subject and the object.

King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if the nature of sentient beings and that of a bodhisattva are non-dual, by what characteristics does a bodhisattva transform and guide sentient beings?"

The intent of the question is as follows: Since the nature of the emanating Bodhisattva and the four types of beings who are emanated is non-dual, by what means of manifestation does he transform sentient beings?
However, the scriptural text states: "If the nature of the Bodhisattva and sentient beings is non-dual..."

This means that one immediately follows the previous instruction not to contemplate the characteristics of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) and not to contemplate the suchness of form (*rūpa-tathatā*). By what characteristic does one transform sentient beings?

One immediately follows the previous instruction that one should abide in this manner to teach and transform those born from the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*). Part Two: The Dual Illumination of Emptiness and Existence. This has two sections.
First, clarifying emptiness by way of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The Buddha said to the Great King: "Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—the dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity—collectively clarify the five aggregates and the four inversions;
all take the dharma-nature as their basis. Having already distinguished that which is observed, I shall next explain that which observes.
One does not dwell in form; one does not dwell in that which is non-form, nor in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
The first two phrases—“not dwelling in form” and “not dwelling in that which is non-form”—pervade the following four aggregates. One does not dwell in feeling, nor in that which is non-feeling;
the remaining three aggregates are to be understood accordingly.
Permanence, bliss, self, and purity: one does not abide in purity, nor does one abide in non-purity.
The latter two phrases—“not abiding in purity” and “not abiding in non-purity”—are governed by the preceding three inversions. One does not abide in permanence, nor does one abide in impermanence;
the remaining two [bliss and self] are likewise.
Why is this? The intent of the inquiry is: for what reason do all things fail to abide? The subsequent explanation states:
because the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is entirely empty.
This refers to the five aggregates and the four inversions; their intrinsic nature is entirely empty. △ Second, clarifying existence by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*):
because of the worldly truth, the preceding phrase provides a general indication, while the following items are listed individually.
Due to three types of designations,
the phenomena (dharma) that are apprehended are called "three.
These are all sentient beings, as well as the phenomena of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).
The five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements;
meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable formations, etc.;
meritorious karma that leads to humans and devas; non-meritorious karma that leads to the four miserable destinies; and the immovable formations, which are the four dhyānas.
These are the four emptinesses. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* clarifies meritorious karma, non-meritorious karma, and immovable karma;
although its text is extensive, it is largely identical to this.
Both cause and effect exist;

this applies universally throughout the three realms. Evil causes lead to suffering results, and wholesome causes lead to blissful results—all are termed "existence" (*bhava*). Above, the six classes of ordinary beings are clarified;
below, the four types of noble ones are distinguished.
The various practices cultivated by the worthies and sages of the three vehicles— namely,
the three stages of worthiness and ten stages of sagehood in the Mahāyāna, and the seven stages of worthiness and four stages of sagehood in the Hīnayāna,
up to the fruit of Buddhahood— are all termed "existence" (bhava).
Next, the sixty-two views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) will be explained in detail.
These are also termed "existence" (*bhava*).
They calculate that the self is form, or they admit that the self is distinct from form, or that the self is within form, or that form is within the self; and so on, up to consciousness.
It is also like this. Calculating four for each of the five aggregates makes twenty; adding the views of past and future, annihilationism and eternalism, they total sixty-two.
△ Third, refuting the question by exposing false discrimination.

Great King, if you are attached to names and characteristics, and conceptually differentiate the dharmas of the six destinies, the four modes of birth, and the practices and fruits of the three vehicles,
then you do not perceive the true nature of all dharmas.
If you conceptually differentiate the two vehicles and the four modes of birth as that which is to be saved, and the fruit of Buddhahood for Bodhisattvas as that which saves, then you do not...

To "see" means to perceive the true nature and reality. △ Second, observing and illuminating to distinguish the wondrous wisdom that can observe, in two parts. First, the question regarding the observer and the observed:
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying: "The true nature of all phenomena is pure and equal; it is neither existent nor non-existent. Wisdom..."
"What is meant by 'shining forth'?
This question intends to ask: if the object of observation is neither existent nor non-existent, how can the observing wisdom shine forth upon both simultaneously?
II. The answer that it is neither empty nor existent has two parts. First, a brief explanation.
The Buddha said, "Great King, wisdom illuminates the true nature, which is neither existent nor non-existent.
By means of the wondrous wisdom of the Middle Way, one illuminates the true nature of reality: not clinging to permanence, it is not 'existent';
not adhering to annihilation, it is not 'non-existent'. The first part is the direct answer; the second part provides the inquiry and explanation.
Why is this so? For what reason is it neither existent nor non-existent?
Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is empty.
Because the nature of all phenomena is ultimate emptiness (paramārtha-śūnyatā). △ Second, the detailed explanation.
Formerly, Xian-shou applied the threefold contemplation of perfect interfusion to the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* and categorized it as belonging to the "Teaching of Reality" (shijiao).

Now, by examining this text, we see that it takes the cause of the wondrous wisdom of a single thought-moment to realize the fruit of the stages and their fulfillment; thus, it belongs to the "Common Teaching of the One Vehicle" (yicheng tongjiao). Therefore, according to [this standard]:
The Patriarch’s Gate of Contemplation explains the purport of the scripture in two sections. First, the contemplation of ultimate emptiness transcending all forms;

second, the contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena. Within the first section, there are four parts. First, the contemplation of returning form to emptiness. Within this, there are three parts. First, clarifying emptiness by way of the objective realm.
These are precisely form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the twelve bases (āyatana); the eighteen elements (dhātu); the six elements of the person;

and earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—these are called the six elements. The section above clarifies the six classes of ordinary beings, while the section below clarifies the four types of noble ones.
The twelve links of dependent origination, the two truths, and the four truths—all are empty.

The two truths are themselves the Middle Way; Bodhisattvas realize this partially, while Tathāgatas realize it to the ultimate degree. The preceding section clearly elucidates the emptiness of the objective realm;
the following section harmonizes this with the emptiness of arising and ceasing.
These dharmas are thus: they arise and they perish simultaneously; they exist and they are empty simultaneously.
They are born in their very place—this is existence. They are extinguished wherever they are—this is emptiness.
Moment by moment, it is likewise so.
In each and every moment, there is both arising and ceasing within emptiness; therefore, it is said, "it is likewise so. The above provides a general explanation.
The sub-commentary explains:
Why is this? Within a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), there are ninety *kṣaṇas*; each *kṣaṇa* undergoes nine hundred arisings and ceasings.
From the subtle to the manifest, these reveal subtle arisings and ceasings that are not cognized by the deluded mind of ordinary beings, nor by those of limited capacity.
Riding upon what is known by those of shallow wisdom, the text concludes at the lower level by stating:
"Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are entirely empty.
If all phenomena were not empty, there would be neither the Path nor its fruit. △ Second, observing emptiness through the lens of wisdom.
By means of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one clearly perceives that all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely empty;

that is to say, by means of the *prajñā* of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), one perceives that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is empty. This is the principle of the two kinds of emptiness, which is what deep wisdom perceives.
The above provides a general explanation; the following provides a detailed enumeration.
Internal emptiness, external emptiness, and internal-external emptiness.
Internal emptiness refers to the six sense faculties; external emptiness refers to the six sense objects;
and internal-external emptiness refers to both together.
The six consciousnesses, arising from the internal faculties and external objects, are also empty;
even this emptiness is empty.
One thoroughly realizes that the eighteen realms are empty, and this very emptiness is also empty.
Great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*). Ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

Great emptiness is identical to equal emptiness (*sama-śūnyatā*); it is the emptiness realized by immovable wisdom. Ultimate emptiness is the principle of signlessness (*animitta*) within the Middle Way;
it is the emptiness that is realized. Equal emptiness is the emptiness of the ten directions.
The emptiness of the conditioned; the emptiness of the unconditioned;
the emptiness of conditioned birth-and-death; the emptiness of unconditioned nirvāṇa;
the emptiness of that which has no beginning; ultimate emptiness; and the emptiness of dispersion.
The past is beginningless emptiness; the future is ultimate emptiness; the present is non-abiding, which is termed the emptiness of dispersion.
There is the emptiness of intrinsic nature and the emptiness of self-characteristics.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is empty of intrinsic nature; the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is empty of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

All phenomena are empty, beginning with the six sense faculties and ending with the two truths. Since all phenomena exist in mutual dependence, they all belong to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); thus, [the text] concludes.
All things are empty. △ Third, both cause and effect are empty.
The Prajñāpāramitā is empty; the cause is empty; the Buddha-fruit is empty.
Since the Prajñā that realizes [enlightenment] is already empty, both the cultivation of the cause and the realization of the fruit are empty.
It is empty because it is the emptiness of emptiness.
Since the various phenomena that are emptied are themselves empty, the wisdom that performs the emptying is also empty. △ Second, the contemplation that emptiness is itself form:
all conditioned phenomena.
These are conditioned phenomena of the mundane and supramundane realms. The above provides a general indication; the following provides a detailed enumeration.
They exist because of the accumulation of dharmas; they exist because of the accumulation of sensation; they exist because of the accumulation of names.
The three are conventional designations (*prajñapti*). Because they are formed through the aggregation of conditions, they are called "origination" (*samudaya*).
Because of the aggregation of causes there is existence; because of the aggregation of fruits there is existence.
These are the Four Noble Truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*). Both mundane and supramundane causes and effects are fully present therein.
They exist because of the six destinies; they exist because of the ten stages; they exist because of the fruit of Buddhahood. All things exist.
Within the cycle of the six destinies, all are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); within the ten stages and the fruit of Buddhahood, all are sages (*ārya*).

Together with the preceding two vehicles and the Four Noble Truths, these constitute the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), all of which exist. △ Third, the contemplation of the non-obstruction between emptiness and form.
"Good son, if a bodhisattva dwells in the marks of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) and possesses the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being,
or a knower, they dwell in the world and are not a bodhisattva."
It is said that this bodhisattva does not understand that the characteristics of form are entirely empty throughout their substance;
therefore, he remains in the world. Why is this? Because all phenomena are entirely empty.
Because form is illusory form, it does not obstruct true emptiness. Thus, the Zhongnan Contemplation states:
"Therefore, when a bodhisattva contemplates form, there is nothing that is not seen as empty. △ Fourth, the contemplation of total extinction and non-reliance.
If one attains immovability regarding all phenomena,
then because the movement of thought and the stirring of mind would immediately mount upon the essence of the Dharma-body,
there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Because it is identical with emptiness, it does not arise; because it is not identical with emptiness, it does not cease.
It is without marks, yet there is no absence of marks.
Because it is identical with illusory form, it is without marks; because it is not identical with illusory form, there is no absence of marks.
One should not give rise to views, nor should one attempt to understand what is seen; this is called the sphere of practice.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are suchness (tathatā), and the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are likewise suchness.
All phenomena are thusness; herein, the principle-dharmadhātu is revealed. △ Second, the contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena.

In the preceding text, form was subsumed into emptiness and emptiness was shown to be identical to form; this was done to eliminate emotional clinging and reveal understanding, demonstrating the non-obstruction between emptiness and form.

Understanding culminates in practice; when all is extinguished and there is no place of reliance, one correctly realizes the essence of practice. Although there are four gates, they together constitute the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Now, in this contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomenon (*dharmatā* and *dharma*), contemplating phenomena corresponds to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), while contemplating principle corresponds to the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

To cause these contemplations to be non-obstructive is precisely to manifest the wondrous function of True Suchness. The text has two parts: first, clarifying the holy realization of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
When noble wisdom manifests, the very first moment is endowed with eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*; this is called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
According to the subsequent scriptural passage, fourteen types of patience (*kṣānti*) are clarified; the Bodhisattva of the first stage practices the *dāna-pāramitā*. Now, [the] supreme...
Regarding the statement that "the first thought-moment is fully endowed with eighty-four thousand [dharmas]": this refers to the wondrous practices of a Bodhisattva, which are of two kinds:

first, sequential arrangement (*xingbu*); second, perfect fusion (*yuanrong*). Sequential arrangement is the provisional establishment of the doctrinal aspects; perfect fusion is the essential nature, principle, virtue, and function.
Because sequential arrangement does not obstruct perfect fusion, the first thought-moment is fully endowed with eighty-four thousand [dharmas]. Perfect...
Fusion does not obstruct sequential arrangement; thus, when a sage of the first stage practices the *dāna-pāramitā*, the *Bhadra-kalpika Sūtra* explains only sequential arrangement.
Only this sūtra and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* possess both [modes] without obstruction.
Therefore, the first stage of that sūtra states: "Within a single stage, all the merits of every stage are fully encompassed. Using this as proof, then now...
This sūtra belongs to the provisional teaching (samaya) of the One Vehicle; its words are not deceptive.

While the preceding section clarified liberation through the exhaustion of hindrances in the first bhūmi, this section distinguishes the remaining nine. That is to say, within each bhūmi, one hindrance and two delusions are abandoned.
One immediately realizes the fruit of liberation.
That which carries [beings] is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*);

that is to say, it carries heavy loads over great distances, and thus it is the Mahāyāna. The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya) of the Liang dynasty also states: "Because it possesses a great nature, it is named [Mahāyāna]."
This constitutes the Mahāyāna. △ Second, the distinction between the two awakenings, Samyaksaṃbodhi and Abhisambodhi:
When the characteristic of movement ceases, it is called the Vajra-samādhi.

The characteristic of movement is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). As the subsequent sutra states: "Contemplating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and severing the characteristic of ignorance—this is [the awakening]."
Perfect enlightenment is likewise attained through the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Its essence and its characteristics are equal, and it is named the "knowledge of all-knowledge" (*sarvajñajñāna*).

One illuminates the essence with fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while one contemplates the characteristics with subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Essence and characteristics are non-dual within their objective sphere; thus, fundamental and subsequent wisdoms [are non-dual].

There is no difference. It is quiescent yet illuminating; is this not what alone constitutes wondrous enlightenment? △ Third, the explanation of the words that elucidate the aforementioned teaching has three parts.
First, the common proclamation by all Buddhas.
"Great King, this Prajñāpāramitā consists of letters, phrases, and the distinctions expressed by those phrases;
'phrases' refers to the interpretation of sentences.
It has been taught in common by hundreds of Buddhas, thousands of Buddhas, and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions—all Buddhas alike."

The path of all Buddhas is identical; what they teach does not differ. The following section, "Chapter on the Practice of Bodhisattvas," describes how the great assembly likewise saw the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges expound the fourteen kinds of patience (*kṣānti*), no different from what our World-Honored One has taught. II. Comparing and Revealing Superiority.
If there were someone who [filled] as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—As the *Kāśyapaparivarta* verse states:
"One thousand sets of four continents, suns and moons, Sumerus, desire-realm heavens, and Brahma-worlds each constitute a small chiliocosm."
This is called a small chiliocosm. A thousand times this small chiliocosm is called a medium chiliocosm. A thousand times this medium chiliocosm is a great trichiliocosm;
all these undergo formation and destruction simultaneously.
If one were to fill [the world] with the seven treasures—
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, agate, red pearls, and crystal—
and use them as a gift for all sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm, such that they all attained the fruit of arhatship;
The former [section] evaluates the measure; the latter reveals its superiority.
It is not equal to someone who, within this sutra, gives rise to even a single thought of pure faith.
Vajra says: "When the mind of faith is pure, then the true mark arises. Therefore, it surpasses the Arhat, whose self-benefit is limited to the partial truth.
How much more so for one who is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite, and understand even a single phrase—
receiving it through the power of faith, upholding it through the power of mindfulness, reading it according to the text, and reciting it apart from the text— and understands that single phrase.
This is not a non-phrase. △ Second, the inquiry and explanation of the reason for this, in two parts.
First, the inquiry:
Why is it that a single thought of pure faith is superior? Why is this so? △ Second, the explanation, in two parts. First, forgetting the expression to attain the essential meaning.
"Supreme!
The nature of letters is detached; they possess no characteristics of letters.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "The nature of letters is detached; there are no letters. This is liberation."
Neither dharma nor non-dharma.
Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Neither dharma" means that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature and characteristics;
"nor non-dharma" means that the true suchness (*tathatā*), which is the real characteristic of selflessness, exists. 2. Revealing the superiority of the person by way of the Dharma.
Because *prajñā* is empty, the bodhisattva is also empty.
The first phrase refers to the dharma; the second phrase refers to the person. Next, it asks and explains:
"Why is this so? Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), each stage possesses birth at the beginning, abiding during the stay, and birth at the end."
The thirty births are all entirely empty.

Seeing the Path for the first time at the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) is called the "birth at the beginning. Cultivating the sublime practices fully within the First Stage is called the "birth during the stay.
When the First Stage is about to be completed and one advances to seek the subsequent stage, it is called the "birth at the end. The same applies to the remaining nine stages.

Taking this as an example, there are thirty [moments], which likewise constitute the three minds—entering, abiding, and emerging—within each stage (*bhūmi*). The above clarifies the emptiness of the cause;
the following illustrates the emptiness of the fruit.
The knowledge of all-knowledge is likewise entirely empty.
The fundamental wisdom of all-knowledge is the "lower wisdom," while the subsequent wisdom follows after the syllables. △ Second, returning the branches to the root to conclude the three points:
first, concluding the teaching expressed by words and letters; second, first, a general indication of the two kinds of false views.
"Great King, if a bodhisattva perceives objects, perceives wisdom, perceives speech, or perceives sensation, these are not the vision of the noble ones; they are the vision of the foolish.
To perceive the object that is the true nature of reality, the wisdom that is contemplative observation, and the verbal expression of sensation—these are not the true vision of noble wisdom."

This is the false view of ordinary fools. △ Second, specifically clarifying the teaching that explains the above, in two parts. First, the three aspects of emptiness regarding the existence of fruits, in three sections.
First, the general heading:
the retributive fruits of sentient beings within the three realms are illusory and false.
The six realms of saṃsāra constitute the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vipāka*) of the world of sentient beings.

The illusory nature of the three realms constitutes the secondary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*) of the receptacle world. However, the term "illusory" encompasses all four evil destinies as well as the four continents and so forth;
thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "All these, too, are summoned and drawn forth by one's own illusory karma. II. Specific Enumeration.
The various karmas produced by the conceptualization of the Desire Realm;

the various karmas produced by the conceptualization of the consciousnesses of the six heavens of the Desire Realm—namely, the cultivation of the ten superior wholesome deeds, as well as giving, precepts, and so forth—"conceptualization" (fenbie) refers to the traces of the mind.
Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Thus, although the forms of these six heavens..."
Setting forth. The traces of mind and body still intermingle.
This is the work performed by the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The heavens of the four dhyānas of the form realm take the dual cultivation of concentration and wisdom as their work: "concentration" refers to tranquil meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and "dhyāna" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*).
Only when concentration and wisdom are balanced can it be called *dhyāna*. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* also states: "Without the support of *dhyāna*, there is no wisdom.
This refers to the karma produced by the four formless *samādhis* of the Sphere of Infinite Space and so forth.

In the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the matter produced as the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) arises, while the matter that is the fruit of karma (*karma-phala-rūpa*) ceases. Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states:

"In these four heavens of emptiness, body and mind are utterly extinguished; the nature of concentration manifests before one, and there is no matter that is the fruit of karma. △ Third, revealing emptiness.
The karmic fruits of the three realms of existence are all empty.

The karmic fruits of evil deeds in the four miserable destinies, the karmic fruits of wholesome deeds among humans and devas, and the karmic fruits of meditative concentration in the higher realms— these causes of the two [lower] realms are empty.
The root of the three realms is ignorance, which is also empty.
All sentient beings within the three realms take ignorance as their root; thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Ignorance is the root of all existence (*bhava*).
Since the fruits of prior karma are already empty, the causes of present delusions are likewise empty. △ Second, concluding the contemplation on the capacity for illumination.
Contemplating the Threefold Subtle Wisdom. First, it clarifies the emptiness of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the various stages of the noble ranks, although there is the arising and ceasing of the untainted (*anāsrava*), the Bodhisattvas on the stages have partially attained untainted wisdom and realized the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing. This is explained comprehensively above.
Regarding the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the following section specifically clarifies the seventh and eighth.
Within the three realms, there remain residual traces of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*).
On the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (*Dūraṃgamā*), one abandons these residual traces of ignorance; thus, the verse below states: "There is no attachment to the dharmas that accord with the Path."
Through clear cultivation, the Bodhisattva of Far-Going alone is able to sever the retribution of transformation;
this, too, is entirely empty.
In the eighth Immovable Stage, one receives the fruit of transformation; the practice of retribution is fully matured, as the following verse says: "The Immovable Bodhi..."
The Bodhisattva of the Second Dhyāna King attains the body of transformation and is eternally sovereign. △ Second, the discernment of the emptiness of Equal Enlightenment:
The Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment attains the Vajra Samādhi; the causes and effects of the two types of death are empty, and all-encompassing wisdom is also empty.
The two types of birth and death—segmented and transformative—are the fruit.

With the two obstacles of afflictions and the known as their cause, once the cause and fruit to be severed are empty, then the omniscience that severs them is likewise empty. △ Third, showing the emptiness of wondrous enlightenment.
The Buddha’s unsurpassed enlightenment is the perfection of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Through the wisdom of analytical discernment, he realizes both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). By means of wisdom, he discriminates and severs the delusions of ignorance; because the fruit of Buddhahood is never severed, it is non-analytical cessation. Thus, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says:

Ignorance is suddenly exhausted; this is called the "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*). The preceding section revealed the fruit of cessation, which is *nirvāṇa*; the following clarifies the fruit of wisdom, which is *bodhi*.
In the true, pure *dharmadhātu*, essence and characteristics are equal, and its functional application is likewise empty.

Nature and characteristics are non-dual; fundamentally there is only the one True Reality. Based on this Truth, the Responsive Manifestation arises to transform all sentient beings. Sentient beings are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*);
thus, all responsive applications are empty. △ Third, concluding with the true nature that is the object of contemplation regarding the reality-mark (*dharmatā*).
Good son, if there are those who practice the Prajñāpāramitā and,
following the aforementioned contemplation,
act as either speaker or listener, they are like illusory beings.
It is the conventional within the ultimate; there is speaking and listening, yet no speaking and no listening.
Phenomena are identical to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), just like empty space.
It is the ultimate within the conventional; there is no speaking and no hearing.
All phenomena are thusness (*tathatā*).

The ultimate and the conventional are non-dual; there is only the single true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). Both mundane and supramundane phenomena are thusness. △ Fifth, a brief indication of protecting the fruit through the causal stage.
"Great King, such is the manner in which a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva protects the fruit of Buddhahood.
Because he protects the fruit of Buddhahood within, he is able to protect the kingdom without; this mutual support between the internal and external is entirely due to Prajñā.
Such is his virtue. 6. Question and Answer: What is the aspect of contemplating the Buddha? Indeed, one who is able to respond to and proclaim the sublime teachings [is so].

Whether their traces were concealed or manifest, they were all Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Now, the general pattern of the dialogue between this sutra and that of Vimalakīrti is entirely identical;

thus, King Bimbisāra may be taken as an analogy for Vimalakīrti. Only in the specific responses do they largely agree with minor differences—essentially, that text is extensive while this one is concise.
The text has three parts. First, the King of Enlightenment (the Buddha) poses the question.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit, saying: "By what marks do you perceive the Tathāgata?
This is entirely identical to the passage in that sutra which asks Vimalakīrti: "If you wish to see the Tathāgata, by what means do you perceive the Tathāgata? Kumārajīva’s commentary states:
"If one possesses the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), one can then illuminate [reality] profoundly; yet, one cannot perceive it [through such means]."
Form. If one lacks the eye of wisdom, then one is separated from form; therefore, he asks: "In what manner does one contemplate the Tathāgata?
△ Second, the Benevolent King’s response, in three parts: first, the general answer.
King Prasenajit said, "Observing the true reality of the body, one observes the Buddha in the same way.
This is identical to what Vimalakīrti said: "As one observes the true reality of one's own body, so one observes the Buddha.
Master Sengzhao’s commentary states: "What is meant by 'Buddha'? It is a title for Great Awakening, having exhausted all principles and perfected one's nature. His Way is void and profound."
Thus, it is truly wondrous and transcends the ordinary realm; the mind cannot be known through wisdom, and its form cannot be measured by images.
It acts as all things do, yet dwells in the domain of non-action; it resides within the sphere of speech and calculation, yet abides in the land beyond words.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "To see the dharma of true reality is to see the Buddha. △ Second, the specific answer. Now, regarding purity...

Within the "Specific Answers" section of the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra), the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva and the two masters Sengzhao and Senglang each presented their own interpretations.
Now, relying on the correct interpretation of our own school, I shall primarily adopt the profound texts of Master Sengzhao while also clarifying their deep and subtle principles.

As for subsuming the sutras according to the teachings, as stated in the following passage—“not abiding in the three periods of time, yet not departing from the three periods of time,” and so forth—all such cases are subsumed under the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhāyāna*).
Neither giving nor stinginess, and so forth—all are subsumed under the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*). This classification is also made according to the text of the *Yanyi chao*.
There is no prior limit, no posterior limit, and no middle limit.
That is to say, the true reality that is contemplated does not come from the past, nor does it go toward the future, nor does it abide in the present;
thus, the three periods of time are extinguished, and this single thought-moment is forgotten.
It does not abide within the three periods of time, nor is it separate from them.
When one seeks the mind within these three periods, the mind is not found and thus does not abide. The three periods of time are entirely present without exception;
they are not separate. This is because time has no distinct substance of its own, and thus there is no abiding; yet because thought-moments and eons are perfectly interfused, there is no separation.
It does not abide in the five aggregates, yet it is not separate from the five aggregates.
Because true form is not distinct from emptiness, it does not abide; because true emptiness is identical to illusory form, it is not separate.
It does not abide in the four great elements, yet it is not separate from the four great elements.
Earth, water, fire, and wind arise through conditions; they do not abide. They are pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm;
they are not separate.
They do not abide in the six sense bases, yet they are not separate from the six sense bases.
Seeing and hearing are like illusions or cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky—this is not abiding in the six sense bases.
Yet, regarding all Tathāgatas, one sees them with constant, vivid clarity—this is not departing from the six sense bases.
One does not dwell within the triple world, yet one does not depart from the triple world.
Because the true mark (*dharmatā*) is pure while the Sahā world is defiled, one does not dwell within the triple world;
yet because the defiled land and the true mark are interfused, one does not depart from the triple world.
It does not abide in any direction, nor does it depart from any direction.

The Dharma-body has no location, yet there is nowhere it is not. Because it has no location, it does not abide in any direction; because there is nowhere it is not, it does not depart from any direction.
Regarding clarity and ignorance, etc., their true mark is signlessness.
Their essence accords with the three types of higher knowledge (vidyā); yet, although the three knowledges exist, they are not different from ignorance.
They are neither identical nor distinct.
It is neither form nor formless; therefore, it is not a single form. Yet, because it is formless, it is not distinct [from form].
It is neither this nor that; neither pure nor defiled.
Abiding in birth and death, it is not this shore; it is not a defiled land. Dwelling in nirvana, it is not the other shore; it is not pure.
The realm is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
If one wishes to call it conditioned, it is without marks and without names; if one wishes to call it unconditioned, it fully responds to the myriad forms.
There is no self-characteristic; there is no other-characteristic.
In the dark and turbid, responding in hidden potential, there is no self-characteristic. In gathering and responding to the realization of truth, there is no other-characteristic.
It is without name and without characteristic.
It cannot be named by names; it cannot be characterized by characteristics.
It is without strength and without weakness; it is without demonstration and without exposition.
Its principle transcends superior wisdom—thus it is without strength and without exposition. Its phenomena dissolve for the lowest of fools—thus it is without weakness and without demonstration.
Neither giving nor stinginess; neither precept-keeping nor transgression; neither patience nor anger; neither diligence nor indolence; neither concentration nor distraction;
neither wisdom nor folly.
The true nature is replete with virtue; it is not something cultivated through the six perfections. Wondrous wisdom is perfectly pervasive; it cannot be obstructed by the six hindrances.
It neither comes nor goes; it neither enters nor exits.
It manifests through the resonance of things; it does not emerge from the royal palace. It conceals itself once the resonance is complete; it does not enter the twin trees.
It is neither a field of merit nor a non-field of merit.
To respond to things without a mind is not to be a field of merit; yet for all who seek, there is benefit, so it is not that one is not a field of merit.
It is neither with marks nor without marks; it is neither grasping nor relinquishing.
Because it is not characterized by marks, it cannot be grasped with a mind of conceptualization; because it is not without marks, it cannot be relinquished through non-thought.
It is neither great nor small; it is neither seen nor heard; it is neither perceived nor known.
It is not small, for when unfolded, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm; thus, it is not something seen by the eyes or heard by the ears of ordinary beings.

It is not large, for when rolled up, it enters into a single speck of dust; thus, it is not something perceived by the bodies or known by the wisdom of those of the Two Vehicles. △ Third, the conclusion and response.
The sphere of mental activity ceases; the path of language is cut off. It is identical to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

Because the sphere of mental activity has ceased, it cannot be conceived by the mind. Because the path of language is cut off, it is equal to the nature of phenomena and cannot be discussed with the mouth.
I observe the Tathāgata by means of these marks;
I observe the Dharma-body Tathāgata by means of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the preceding text states: "Observing the true mark of the body, observing the Buddha is likewise.
△ Third, refuting heterodoxy by citing examples of seals.

The Buddha said, "Good son, it is as you have said. The powers, fearlessnesses, and other such qualities of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas—merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and all their unique attributes—are entirely like this."

It is as you have said. When one contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Buddha, it is free from all that is non-existent; likewise, the powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth of the Buddhas are also free from what is non-existent.
Therefore, it is said that "all are thus. This refers to the merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and the various unshared qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
This refers to the Tathāgata’s one hundred and forty unique qualities (*āveṇika-guṇa*). The upper [section] provides the model; the lower [section] refutes error.
Those who cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā* should contemplate in this manner.
By means of the wondrous wisdom of contemplative observation, one darkly accords with the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
If one observes otherwise, it is called "erroneous observation.
Apart from the true nature of reality, everything else is the work of Māra; therefore, it is called erroneous observation. △ Seventh: Summary of the Benefits Attained by the Assembly at That Time.
Furthermore, when this Dharma was being taught, an immeasurable great assembly attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Examining this text closely, it concludes the sixth [section] proximately and the preceding five distantly; from the beginning to the end, it universally concludes the one.

In this chapter, those who attain the purity of the Dharma-eye are likewise described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Upon hearing the teaching on the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*), they become distant from dust and free from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye;

this is precisely the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) of the First Ground (*prathamā-bhūmi*). However, when Master Sengzhao commented on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, he stated that attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye corresponds to the stage of the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
That was because he was referring to the manifestation of the Buddha’s land as adorned and pure, and the various devas...
Furthermore, he understood that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely impermanent and thereby attained the benefits of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
Compared to the Great Teaching of the present day, his [attainment] is like the glow of a firefly vying for brilliance with the bright sun.
Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll One;
Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan, who transmits the teachings of the Patriarch Xianshou in the Great Song State.
Chapter Three: The Practice of the Bodhisattva.

Regarding the explanation of this chapter, the three introductory sections are the same as before. First, concerning the intent of its arrival: the preceding chapter has already protected the fruit of Buddhahood, while this chapter protects the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Since the qualities of the fruit have been manifested, the causal practices are now about to be set forth; therefore, it follows in sequence. Second, the explanation [of the title].
The name consists of two parts: *bodhi*, which is translated as "awakening" (*jue*), and *sattva*, which means "sentient being" (*zhòngshēng*).

This refers to seeking supreme awakening through wisdom while saving sentient beings below through compassion; thus, it derives its name from its objective. In this way, where there is compassion, one acts in accordance with phenomena (*xiàng*);
where there is wisdom, one acts apart from phenomena. When compassion and wisdom guide one another, they constitute the practice of non-abiding. However...
