As for the Dharma-gates that are taught: if one says they are one, each according to their kind understands them differently; it is not that the true nature is one. If one says they are infinite, they are all expounded by a single voice;
it is not that there are as many [voices] as there are sentient beings. Part Two: Investigation and Explanation (divided into two).
First, the inquiry:
For what reason?
Why is it neither one nor manifold? △ Second, the explanation, which has two parts. First, regarding the difference in the characteristics of the faculties while their nature is one.
Based on the characteristics of the five aggregates of clinging— comprising the physical phenomena (rūpa-dharma) and mental phenomena (citta-dharma)— of all sentient beings,
they falsely grasp at the characteristic of the aggregates by combining physical form into one and dividing the mind into four.
They then conceive of various roots, activities, and categories, such as self, person, knowledge, and views, which are infinite in their variety.
Deluded knowledge and deluded views differ according to the varying capacities of beings; their practices and traces are not the same, and their categories are boundless.
Accordingly, the Dharma gates that accord with these capacities are likewise immeasurable.
The Dharma gates bestowed [upon beings] are also immeasurable, according to their faculties and following their respective tracks of practice;
the former clarifies their differences in appearance, while the latter demonstrates their oneness in nature.
The nature of these dharmas is neither with marks nor without marks, yet it is not without measure.
Indeed, the nature of dharmas is singular; it is neither with marks, nor without marks, nor is it characterized by immeasurable marks.
△ Second, distinguishing the True One and the Conventional Two according to the Truths (*satya*). First, the exclusion of what is not.
If a bodhisattva follows the perceptions of sentient beings, they may perceive [reality] as one or two;
if a bodhisattva follows ordinary perception, they distinguish between the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), which is unique, and the conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya), which possesses both.
This is precisely not seeing the meaning of "one" and "two," nor seeing the Middle Way.
It is that the mundane does not contradict the one reality of the True, and the True does not contradict the two aspects of the mundane. △ Second, revealing what this is.
To understand "one and two" as being neither one nor two is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
To understand "one" as the single true truth (*tattvasatya*) and "two" as the dual conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), and to realize that which is neither true nor conventional,
is the Middle Way of the ultimate truth.
To grasp at and cling to "one" or "two," whether as existence or non-existence, is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

This serves to reveal by contrast that clinging to "one" is clinging to the ultimate, while clinging to "two" is clinging to the conventional; for these two dharmas—existence and non-existence—are precisely the conventional truth.
This is also the same as the *Buzhenkong lun* (Treatise on the Non-emptiness of Reality). Although existence and non-existence differ, both are merely conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
△ Second, the comprehensive conclusion: Therefore, this Dharma-gate is neither one nor two.
This concludes the preceding section on the Dharma-gate that was bestowed; it is neither one nor is it infinite. △ Fourth, the simultaneous teaching by all Buddhas, which consists of four parts.
First, taking one Buddha as an example for many:
"Great King, all Buddhas preach the Prajñāpāramitā."
First, I shall cite the examples.
I now teach the Prajñāpāramitā as being without duality and without distinction;
its fruit is non-dual, and its teaching is undifferentiated.
"You, the great assembly, should receive, uphold, read, and recite this, and practice according to what is taught; this is itself the upholding of the Dharma of all Buddhas.
Part Two: Revealing the Abundance of Merit. Section One: Clarifying the Abundance of Those Capable of Explaining It.
"Great King, this Prajñāpāramitā possesses immeasurable merit;
it is designated as having great merit.
Suppose there were unspeakably many Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The Buddhas who are able to manifest emanations are many;
each and every one of these Buddhas teaches and transforms immeasurable, ineffable numbers of sentient beings,
and the number of sentient beings thus transformed is vast.
Each and every sentient being attains Buddhahood.
When these sentient beings have attained the fruit,
these Buddhas and others, in turn, teach and transform immeasurable and unspeakable numbers of sentient beings, who likewise all attain Buddhahood.
Successively, many have attained Buddhahood. △ Second, revealing the abundance of what was taught:
The Prajñāpāramitā taught by these Buddhas and others consists of immeasurable, unspeakable *nayuta* billions of verses; it cannot be fully expounded.
This refers to the successive attainment of the Way. Each and every Buddha has expounded as many verses as there are, which are inexhaustible;
"nayuta" is translated here as one hundred million. △ Third, citing the few to illustrate the many.

Among all the verses, if one were to take a single verse and divide it into a thousand parts, and then explain only one part of those thousand parts, the merit of its phrasing and meaning would still be inexhaustible;
how much more so, then, for the merit inherent in such immeasurable phrases and meanings?
Even the merit described in a single phrase cannot be exhausted; how much less can that of immeasurable phrases be fathomed?
△ Fourth, the comparison of the superiority of the great [merit], in two parts. First, showing that a single moment of faith transcends suffering.
If there is anyone who can give rise to even a single thought of pure faith in this sutra, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"To have no faith in any phenomena is to have faith in Prajñā."
Such a person will immediately transcend the suffering and hardships of birth and death for hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, and hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas.
△ Second, how much more so for those who practice the four dharmas to attain bliss;
how much more so for those who copy, receive and uphold, read and recite, and explain them to others.
The merit obtained through these four modes of practice is equal to that of all Buddhas of the ten directions, without any difference.
Above, it accords with the bliss of the tranquility of Nirvana; below, it accomplishes the bliss of awakening to the Dharma of Bodhi.
It should be known that this person is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas and will before long attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
△ Fifth, awakening to the Way upon hearing the Dharma.
When this Dharma was being taught, ten billion people attained the patience of the three emptinesses;
the bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness attained the emptiness of the three provisional designations;
and one hundred trillion people attained the patience of great emptiness.
Fourth, the Bodhisattvas in the stage of application (prayoga) universally realize the emptiness of the ten directions.

Immeasurable Bodhisattvas attain the ten stages (bhūmi), beginning with the Stage of Joy (pramuditā) and culminating in the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā), entering each stage through successive realization. △ Next, three chapters of the main text distinguish [these matters].

Regarding external protection: first, the "Chapter on Protecting the Nation" (Rāṣṭrapāla-parivarta) primarily elucidates external protection; second, the "Chapter on the Inconceivable" (Acintya-parivarta) presents external protection concurrently;
third, the "Chapter on Upholding" (Parindana-parivarta) expands upon these two forms of protection. Now, for the first, which primarily elucidates external protection.
Regarding the introductory intent of the fifth chapter, "Protecting the State":
The preceding three chapters have fully elucidated cause and effect, collectively constituting internal protection (*adhyātma-rakṣā*).

Since internal protection has already been manifested, external protection (*bāhya-rakṣā*) ought now to be revealed; therefore, this chapter follows. Second, regarding the explanation of the title: it has already been interpreted in the commentary on the sutra’s title.
Guohu: Regarding the meaning of "protection," I have personally attempted to investigate its origins. There is mundane protection and supramundane protection.
Why is this? For the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, supported by compassion and wisdom, sprinkle the rain of the Dharma to rescue and protect all classes of beings.

This is supramundane protection. Holy emperors, enlightened kings, the five ranks of nobles, and the hundred officials—rulers and ministers who protect the Dharma and nurture the common people—this is mundane protection.
In both the mundane and supramundane realms, their virtues are identical.

If even Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the eight classes of devas and nāgas bestow their blessings, how much more so regarding the three calamities and seven difficulties; how could they possibly fail to preserve [the world]?
"Is it not imperishable? △ Third, the explanation of the scripture has four parts. First, the command to listen and permission to speak:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit and the other great kings: "Listen attentively, listen attentively!
For your sakes, I shall expound the Dharma for protecting the state."
This single recitation of the sutra serves as a response to the initial request made by the various kings in the "Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata.
Thus, the preceding text states: "I know that the sixteen kings and others all had this thought: 'The World-Honored One possesses great compassion and brings benefit and happiness to all.
How, then, shall we, the various kings, protect our kingdoms? This is identical to the section in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* concerning the interlacing and mutual regard [of the kings]. Chapter...

The threefold request was likewise answered with spoken words. However, although the Buddha already knew that the King requested protection for the state, he first spoke of protecting the fruit of Buddhahood and those who practice the ten stages (bhūmi).
This means that if there were no internal protection of cause and effect, external calamities would have no way to be completely extinguished;
therefore, he first spoke of internal protection and subsequently spoke of external protection. II. The Actual Exposition.
The third [section] concerns the protection of the state. First, it clarifies the time of protection:
when all lands—meaning all territories governed by various kings—are about to fall into disorder, this also refers to the disorder occurring within the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).

The world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) is that which is protected. As the sutra below states: "The earth and heavens undergo strange transformations," which refers to the disorder of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*);
"the common people perish," which refers to the disorder of the world of sentient beings. Furthermore, it says:
"Place one hundred Buddha images," etc., referring to the world of the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyak-saṃbuddha-loka*) as the protector.
There are various calamities and perils. "Calamities" refers to the three great calamities;
"perils" refers to the seven perils. There are two kinds of thieves: first, external bandits and robbers; second, the internal thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
There are also two kinds of protection: first, the assembly of spirits and deities; second, the teaching of Prajñā. By means of the assembly of spirits and deities...
They eliminate the thieves of the kalpa through the teaching of Prajñā; they eliminate the thieves of affliction through Prajñā. △ Second, showing the protection of the Dharma has three parts.
First, propagating the sutra and enshrining images:
"You kings, you should receive, uphold, read, and recite this Prajñāpāramitā, and adorn the path."
In that place, one should set out one hundred Buddha images, one hundred Bodhisattva images, and one hundred lion thrones, and invite one hundred Dharma masters to expound this sutra.
The reason for setting out one hundred Buddha and Bodhisattva images each is not merely to represent the destination and the direction toward which the one hundred Dharma masters turn.

This means that the Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata is taken as the protection of the fruit, for which an image of the Buddha is placed; the Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Practice is taken as the protection of the cause, for which an image of a bodhisattva is placed.
Therefore, one first places the images representing the internal protection of cause and fruit, and subsequently invites one hundred Dharma masters to expound the teachings of external protection.
This is merely a symbolic representation. Nevertheless, in recent times, people have followed the sutras in establishing the assembly of one hundred Dharma masters.
He convened a meeting and immediately invited one hundred monks to recite the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

He considered that both the *Renwang jing* and the *Guangming jing* were sutras of the Dharma King, just as the *Zhouyi* and the *Maoshi* are the teachings of the "Plain King" (Confucius); in their benefit to sentient beings, they are all the same.
I shall now employ a proximate analogy to illustrate a remote principle. Consider ice and water: their moist nature is identical.

When melted, they become water; when frozen, they become ice. If one follows the Buddha’s words and invites a hundred monks to recite the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is like melting ice to form water—the return to the source is not far off.
Yet, to rebel against the Sage’s intention and instead invite [monks] from various quarters...
To don the robes and recite the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is like boiling water in search of ice—is it not difficult?
Nevertheless, by studying the *Book of Changes*, one investigates purity and subtle refinement; by mastering the *Book of Poetry*, one explores gentleness and profound sincerity.

If both scriptures benefit beings in the same way, what difference is there between teaching gentleness and profound sincerity through the *Poetry* and [achieving] purity and subtle refinement through the *Changes*?
To be pure, refined, and subtle—this is the sole aspiration for those who possess the Way. To reform vulgar failings and follow the sagely teachings is my earnest wish.
△ Second, the full arrangement of ritual offerings.
Before each of the seats, they lit various lamps, burned various incenses, and scattered various flowers as a vast offering.

For lamps, they used ghee and wax; for incense, they burned aloeswood and sandalwood. In spring and summer, they scattered flowers of grasses and trees; in the cold of winter, they scattered flowers of silk and brocade.
Robes, bedding, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, dwellings, and seats—these constitute all forms of service.
The *Lanpen shu* (Lan-pen Commentary) states that one should provide for the Three Honored Ones with these four requisites: dwellings, robes, food and drink, and medicinal decoctions.
These additions of bedding and seats are merely the necessary provisions for the dwelling. △ Third, regarding the conditions for preaching and listening while removing obstacles:

if twice daily one lectures on or reads this sutra, and if kings, ministers, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās listen to, receive, read, and recite it, practicing according to the Dharma, then calamities and disasters will immediately be extinguished.

Furthermore, as for the wondrous wisdom and the true exposition, although it relies upon daily exhortation and encouragement, it does not employ the mental activities of arising and ceasing to preach the Dharma-gate of the True Mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
This lies in the simultaneous flow of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, whereby one may purify the three calamities and wash away the seven hardships.
Thus, among a hundred lecture halls, only a single seat is established within the imperial palace, where the Great King [resides].

Your servant [the Emperor] has fully and sincerely listened. All others have been dispersed to separate lodgings within the capital region and throughout the various provinces, so that monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen may hear this and put it into practice.
Therefore, it is said: "Listen, receive, read, and recite, and practice according to the Dharma."
△ Third, the manifestation of the benefits of protection, in three parts. First, a general explanation of the capacity for protection:
"Great King, within all lands there are immeasurable spirits and ghosts, each with their own immeasurable retinues.
If they hear this sutra, they will protect your land."

Each seat has its own infinite number of presiding deities. Therefore, it is fitting that the speaker exerts himself to expound the ultimate teaching, so that the Dharma may be honored and the person [the teacher] respected;
thus, the True Dharma will abide for a long time. △ Second, the specific enumeration of those who provide protection, in two parts.
First, the distinction between the hidden and the manifest is set forth:

if a state is about to fall into chaos, the ghosts and spirits will first fall into chaos; because the ghosts and spirits are in chaos, the myriad people will immediately fall into chaos, and bandits shall arise.

The death of the common people and the confusion of spirits and deities arise from two causes and conditions. First, when a king destroys the Triple Gem, the celestial deities do not grant their protection;
pestilence and malevolent ghosts come daily to inflict harm. Second, when the king’s merit is exhausted, all the sages [withdraw their support].

All shall depart. The seven calamities will inevitably arise. According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, if one raises an army to wage war out of greed for territory, many will die unjustly, and the common people will perish.
Subsequently, virtuous deities will leave the realm, and malevolent spirits will bring about disasters;
thus, bandits shall surely rise. △ Second, listing the primary and secondary [retributions].
The king’s crown prince and the princes of the various officials disputed with one another over right and wrong.
According to Han regulations, the son of the Emperor was called the Crown Prince (Taizi), while the sons of the feudal lords were called the Heir Apparent (Shizi).
Their mutual disputations were like the "Witchcraft Incident" (Wugu) of the Han dynasty.

Heaven and earth undergo strange transformations; the sun, moon, and the multitude of stars lose their proper seasons and degrees; great fires, great floods, and great winds arise—these various calamities emerge.
The phrasing belongs to this chapter, while the meaning connects to the following sentence. △ Third, the benefit derived from the teaching, in two parts.
First, when difficulties arise while upholding and expounding the scriptural text, one should in all cases uphold, recite, and study this *Prajñāpāramitā*.
When strange and difficult circumstances compete to arise, the cultivation of virtue can ward them off; as the saying goes: "Even if Heaven sends down calamity, it may still be averted. △ Second.
II. Attaining Merit and Dispelling Difficulties. First, attaining merit:
If one receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra, all that is sought—official rank, wealth and abundance, sons and daughters, and wisdom and understanding—will be attained.
One may come and go as one pleases, and the karmic rewards of humans and devas shall all be fully attained.
If, regarding this sutra, one receives, maintains, reads, and recites even two lines, one will penetrate the beginning of the removal of difficulties. △ Second, the removal of difficulties.
Epidemics and calamities shall be immediately cured; those whose bodies are bound by cangues, shackles, or fetters shall all attain liberation;
and even those who have violated the four grave precepts or committed the five heinous crimes [shall be purified].

The four grave offenses are: sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying. The five heinous crimes are: killing one’s father, harming one’s mother, killing an arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
"And the destruction of the various precepts.

The word "and" (*ji*) has two meanings. First, it distinguishes from the preceding meaning to clarify that there are two matters: namely, while the preceding section clarified the four fundamental grave offenses (*mūlāpatti*), this section clarifies the remaining minor rules (*śeṣa-apatti*).
Second, it has the sense of a collective inclusion; it indicates not only the violation of the light and heavy [offenses] of the Hīnayāna, but also...
Because one has violated the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts of the Mahāyāna, it is said here that "all precepts" are meant. The preceding lines list them individually;
the final phrase summarizes them:
"immeasurable transgressions shall all be extinguished."
△ Third, citing three examples from the past concerning the protection of the kingdom. First, citing the Heavenly King:
"Great King, in the distant past, Śakra Devānām Indra was King Mūrdhaja."
"Of" (*wei*) is equivalent to "donning" (*bei*).
To lead the fourfold host—
elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry— is also termed the "fourfold army" (*sibing*).
He came to the celestial palace with the desire to overthrow Śakra.

"Śakra-devānām-indra" is the term in the language of India; in this region [China], he is called the "Lord of Heaven Capable of Nurturing and Exhorting to Goodness," because he is capable of acting as the Lord of Heaven.
There is yet another interpretation of "Śakra," as found in the *Huayan yinyi* (Explanations of Terms in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra).
Then that Lord of Devas, following the teachings of the Buddhas of the past, prepared a hundred high seats and invited a hundred Dharma masters to lecture and recite the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Thereupon, Māndhātṛ retreated, and the hosts of devas were brought peace and happiness.

The heavenly beings possess sovereign bliss and their majestic radiance is exceptionally venerable; yet they still revere Prajñā and request its protection. How much more so for a king of men—who would not practice and honor it?
However, Śakra also preached the Dharma-gate of the Ten Wholesome Paths in the Hall of Good Dharma, but it was only for the sake of the celestial hosts.
△ Second, citing the example of the human king, in two parts. First, Bāṇa relying on heterodox teachings, in two parts. First, the fault.
Regarding false teachers:
Great King, in the past, King Tiṣya-rāja had a crown prince named Pāda-paṅka (Spotted-foot).
He was given that name because his feet were mottled. Both the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* recount this account.
When he ascended the throne, there was a non-Buddhist teacher named Śubhadatta who conferred the consecration upon the king;
because his realization reached the subtle and the pervasive, it was termed "the Way" (mārga), yet his mind wandered outside of that Way, so he was called a "non-Buddhist" (tīrthika).
When the crown prince of a Wheel-turning King (cakravartin) was about to ascend the throne, he likewise took seawater to pour over his head in consecration.
He then commanded Pañcaśikha to take the heads of the thousand kings and offer them at the cemetery;
because he sacrificed there without ceasing, it was called Śmaśāna (the Cemetery).
Mahākāla is the Great Black Deity.
The first phrase is in Sanskrit; the second phrase is in Chinese (Táng-yán), translated as Mahākāla. Śiva is the deity of war.

According to the *Xiányú jīng* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish), he is worshipped as a rākṣasa king; according to the *Duànròu jīng* (Sūtra on Abstaining from Meat), he is worshipped as a mountain deity. △ Second, taking the Thousand Kings.
Since ascending the throne, he has already obtained nine hundred and ninety-nine kings;
lacking only one king, he traveled ten thousand *li* to the north and finally obtained one, named Puming.
The *Pumingwang Jing* (Sūtra of King Puming) and the *Duannrou Jing* (Sūtra on Prohibiting Meat) both state that one hundred kings were selected. II. Puming Adheres to the True Dharma.
This section has four parts. First, the presentation of his vow and its acceptance.
King Puming spoke to the White-footed One, saying: "I pray that you will permit me for one day to pay homage to the Triple Gem and provide food for the śramaṇas."
Having heard this, Pādapāṇi immediately granted his consent.
Second, the preparation of seats and the invitation to preach:
The king then followed the teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the past; he prepared one hundred high seats and invited one hundred Dharma masters.
Twice each day, he preached eight billion verses of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

△ Third, the actual recitation of the verses: from among those eight billion verses, he cited eight stanzas on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, so that the King and his retinue might realize and witness emptiness. This was heard by others in succession.
It is for the benefit of the ears. The text has two parts. First, identifying the speaker:
at that time, the foremost Dharma Master among the assembly spoke these verses to King Samantaprabha.
△ Second, the four verses of the formal exposition.
First, the manifestation of impermanence: "The kalpa-fire blazes fiercely; the great trichiliocosm is destroyed together.

"Kalpa" refers to the *saṃvarta-kalpa* (the eon of destruction). That which brings about destruction consists of the three calamities (*trividha-vipatti*). Here, only the calamity of fire is mentioned; thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says: "This..."
A thousand small chiliocosms constitute a great trichiliocosm; all are subject to the same process of formation and destruction.
Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans are completely worn away until nothing remains.
"Sumeru" is fully called *Sumeru*; here it means "Wondrously High and Massive. Above, the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) is destroyed; below, [the sentient world is destroyed].
The world of sentient beings—Brahmās, Śakras, devas, nāgas, and all such beings.
"Brahmā" refers to Brahmā-rāja, encompassing the celestial kings of the four dhyānas. "Śakra" refers to Śakra-devendra, the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. [This] is mentioned...

This includes all other devas; devas and nāgas comprise the eight classes of beings. Since even all sentient beings—namely those of the six destinies and four modes of birth—are to be utterly extinguished, how much more so this body?

Within the three realms there is superiority and inferiority; within the six destinies there is suffering and joy. Since all these are subject to destruction and extinction, how much more so one's own single body?
Part two: Proclaiming the Eight Sufferings.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death;

sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—these four sufferings, within the desire realm, follow one in pursuit of adverse conditions; sorrow and lamentation cut deeply into one another, while suffering and affliction overwhelm each other.
Being oppressed by enemies and loved ones can thwart one's wishes:

"enemies" refers to the suffering of encountering what is hateful; "loved ones" refers to the suffering of separation from what is dear; and "oppression" refers to the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
They can thwart one's wishes; there is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
The fetters and latent tendencies of craving create sores for oneself. There is no peace within the three realms; what joy can there be in this kingdom?
Ignorance and craving, the nine fetters and ten proclivities—these are the causes for the production of karma. Having oneself performed the actions, one suffers the bitter fruits thereof.
Like a festering sore or a tumor, all three realms are suffering; what joy can there be in a single land? △ Third, the teaching on the emptiness of phenomena.
Conditioned phenomena are unreal; they arise from causes and conditions. They wax and wane like a flash of lightning; having momentarily existed, they cease to be.
Conditioned dharmas are false and insubstantial; they arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions. When conditions assemble, they flourish;
when conditions disperse, they decay. They are like a flash of lightning: arising for a brief moment, they immediately perish.
The various realms, destinies, and births manifest according to the conditions of karma; they are like shadows and echoes, all of which are empty.
The superior and inferior locations within the three realms are produced by collective karma, while the bodies of suffering and pleasure in the six destinies are produced by individual karma.
Just as images appear in a clear mirror and echoes respond in an empty valley, all phenomena that exist are ultimately [empty].
Emptiness. △ Fourth, the elucidation of non-self:
Consciousness is drifted by karma and arises riding upon the four great elements. Bound by ignorance and craving, the notions of "self" and "mine" arise.
This means that the aggregate-retribution consciousness is drifted and moved by karma, and riding upon those four great elements, it arises as the physical form of the body. Within, there is no...
One clearly perceives that within the five aggregates, one clings to them as a self; externally, bound by craving, one gives rise to the notion of "mine" regarding the resources of the kingdom.
Consciousness migrates according to karma, and the body is thus without a master. One should know that the realm of the country is likewise an illusory transformation.
The prior retributive consciousness then migrates according to karma to take birth in other realms; thus, it is without a master.

Since the primary retribution has already transmigrated, one should know that the dependent retribution—the lands and environments—is likewise an illusory transformation. △ Fourth, the benefits obtained from the verses, in five parts:
first, the benefit of the verse received by Puming.
At that time, after the Dharma Master had spoken these verses, King Samantaprabha heard the Dharma and attained realization, realizing the *śūnyatā-samādhi*.
Had he heard the preceding verses, he would have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), because they concern the aspects of the Truth of Suffering, such as impermanence.
Alternatively, having heard the Dharma and realized emptiness, he understood the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and immediately reached the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).
The king and his retinue attained the emptiness of the Dharma-eye.
Subsequently, the king attained realization and reached the stage of the Ten Faiths. II. The Benefit of the Kings Reciting Verses:
The king then proceeded to the kingdom of Tārā. In the midst of the assembly of kings, he spoke these words: "O virtuous ones, now..."
When the time for the ritual comes, one should recite and maintain the verses on the *prajñāpāramitā* spoken by the Buddhas of the past;
that is, the aforementioned eight verses.
Upon hearing this, all the kings also attained awakening and understanding; they realized the Samādhi of Emptiness and each recited and upheld [the teaching].
By reciting the verses, they awakened to the underlying principle, just as King Puming did. △ Third, the benefit of Banzu hearing the verses.
At that time, King Pādapāṇi asked the kings, "What teachings are you all currently reciting?
Since the conditions for Pādapāṇi’s past karma had ripened, he questioned them in order to discern [their knowledge].
At that time, Samantaprabha replied to King Pādapāṇi with the above verses. Upon hearing this Dharma, the king also realized the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
This concentration of emptiness is the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*). △ Fourth, the account of the error, the return to the kingdom, and the benefits.
Rejoicing and leaping for joy, he addressed the kings, saying: "I have been misled by heterodox teachers; this is not your fault.
Internally joyful yet externally exultant, he thus reproached himself.
"Each of you shall return to your respective kingdoms and invite Dharma Masters to expound upon the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
By transforming others through successive transmission, the benefits of the Dharma will be inexhaustible. △ 5. The benefit of leaving home and attaining realization.

At that time, King Pāṇḍupāda entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother and left the household life to pursue the Way. He attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (receptivity to the non-arising of phenomena) and immediately realized the first stage (*bhūmi*).

However, as for this non-Buddhist practitioner Pāṇḍupāda, he may have practiced "inner secrecy and outer manifestation," employing both contrary and compliant methods in his transformative traces (*vṛtti*) in order to cause the holy teaching to spread its fragrance.
How could this be something to be conceived by the petty minds of ordinary people or discussed with the mouths of the mundane? △ Third, the analogy of various kings, in three parts.
First, citing the past:
"Great King, in the past there were five thousand kings who constantly recited this sutra and obtained its rewards in their present lives.
Because they constantly recited and upheld it, they received these manifest retributions. Second, citing the present.
"You sixteen great kings who cultivate the Dharma for protecting the state should likewise receive, uphold, recite, and explain this sutra.
You should invite one hundred Dharma masters as previously described. △ Third, an analogy for the future.
If, in future ages, there should be kings and others who wish to protect their nations and protect themselves, they too should likewise receive,
uphold, recite, and explain this sutra.

Thus, having grasped the main principles and raised the collar, the teachings of the Three Ages have been proclaimed; as the Dharma is practiced and the sublime regulations honored, the renown of the ten thousand nations awaits its dissemination.
△ Fourth, awakening to the Way upon hearing the Dharma.
When this Dharma was being taught, immeasurable multitudes of people attained the stage of non-retrogression.
There are four types of non-retrogression: those of faith, practice, and realization, each according to what is appropriate for them.
The asuras and others were reborn in the heavens;
together with the other seven classes, they all ascended.
Immeasurable and innumerable devas of the desire and form realms attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas of the first stage attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
△ The second major section, the "Inconceivable Chapter," also presents the protection of the state.
Regarding the introductory intent of the sixth chapter, "The Inconceivable":
In the preceding chapter, the *Prajñāpāramitā* was expounded by a hundred lecturers; the state was protected, the people were pacified, and all calamities were extinguished.
This chapter follows next because it offers flowers to manifest the wondrous purport of *prajñā*, whose merit is profound and difficult to fathom. (2)

Explanation of Terms: Furthermore, the inconceivable (*acintya*) is briefly of two kinds: first, the inconceivability of its virtuous attributes (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*); second, the inconceivability of its functional activity (*karma-vṛtti*).
As clarified in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, "Dust motes contain the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), their measure equaling that of empty space"—this is the inconceivability of its virtuous attributes.

In the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, it is said that "a single hair swallows the great ocean" and "a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru"—this is the inconceivability of its functional activity. Now, regarding this sūtra...
The World-Honored One manifested inconceivable supernatural transformations for the great assembly;
even an immeasurable great ocean entered a single pore, and immeasurable Mount Sumerus entered a mustard seed. These are the inconceivable functions of karma;
they are all beyond the path of language and where the movements of the mind cease. This is likewise as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: that which cannot be proclaimed by words.
It is not something that can be fathomed by the mind alone. Dharma Master Bihai further stated that there are two kinds of the inconceivable (*acintya*):
first, the internal essence, which refers to the true reality (*dharmatā*). When one wishes to speak of it with the mouth, words fail; when the mind attempts to take it as an object, thought ceases.

Second, the external traces, which refer to the mutual containment of the vast and the minute, and the simultaneous response to diverse forms. However, the profound gate is difficult to open, and the manifestations of the sages vary accordingly.
Without the fundamental (hon), there would be no way to manifest the traces (jaku); without the traces, there would be no way to reveal the fundamental.

Although the fundamental and the traces differ, they are one in their inconceivability. The commentary states: although this clarifies the internal fundamental and external traces, it primarily elucidates the functioning of karmic activity; thus, it belongs to the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching (dōgyō ichijō).

Yet, as it involves the characteristics of virtue (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*), it is merely the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*). △ Third, the explanation of the sūtra has four parts.

First, rejoicing upon hearing the Dharma: At that time, the sixteen kings and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha speak these profound phrases and meanings of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
As heard in the preceding chapter, both the protection of the state in the past and present has always been due to the *prajñāpāramitā*.

This section likewise follows upon the previous account of hearing the Dharma to initiate the subsequent scattering of flowers; therefore, the general heading states: "Also describing the protection of the state. II. The Great Assembly Scatters Flowers.
First, the flowers form a jeweled throne (in three parts). A. The scattering of flowers forms the throne.
One scatters hundreds of thousands of millions of various precious lotus flowers.

If interpreted according to the symbolic teaching of the Dharma, this refers to Bodhisattvas prior to the stages of the grounds who, relying on the *prajñā* of words and letters, cultivate the causes while remaining unstained by the fruits.
In the midst of empty space, a precious lotus throne is formed, signifying that all phenomena are empty and serving as the basis for practice. △ Second, the Buddhas sit and preach the Dharma.
The Buddhas of the ten directions...
This represents the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata and the immeasurable great assembly.
According to the *Zaoyao*, this corresponds to the stage of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*).
They sat together upon this seat and preached the Prajñāpāramitā.
△ Third, forming a wheel with flowers:
this great assembly took ten thousand golden lotus flowers and scattered them over Śākyamuni Buddha.
In the Sanskrit language, *Śākyamuni* is translated as "Capable Benevolent One" (*Nengren*) and "Silent and Still" (*Jimo*).
Combined, these form a lotus wheel that covers the great assembly.
The first phrase signifies that the Wheel of Dharma has already been turned; the second phrase signifies that those who hear the Dharma obtain benefit. △ Second, flowers become clouds.
The third terrace: First, flowers were scattered to form a terrace;
then, eighty-four thousand *puṇḍarīka* flowers—these being white lotuses—were scattered again by the King and others.
Hence, it says "again. This represents the initial vision of the path on the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
In a single thought-moment, one possesses eighty-four thousand pāramitās.
In the midst of empty space, a white cloud pavilion is formed, symbolizing the prajñā of contemplative observation.
It shatters the darkness of ignorance, so that the nature of reality is seen with clarity and brightness. The subsequent sutra also says: "For example..."
There is a person who ascends the great high seat, which is the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*); here, it specifically represents the noble ones of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
△ Second, preaching the Dharma within the platform.
Within the platform is the Buddha King of Radiance (*Prabhāpāla*), together with the Buddhas of the ten directions.
This represents the *saṃbhogakāya* for the enjoyment of others;
it is for the sake of the immeasurable great assembly,
as exemplified in the *Zaoyao*, so that others may joyfully realize the Way.
He preached the Prajñāpāramitā.
With a single voice he preached, yet each according to their kind understood it. △ Third, offering flowers to the Buddha:
this great assembly held māndārava flowers.
*Mandala*. In this region [of China], it is called "that which accords with the mind.
It was scattered over Śākyamuni Buddha and the entire assembly.
△ Third, the flowers form a jeweled city. Part two: First, the scattering of flowers to form a city.
Furthermore, he scattered mañjuṣaka flowers—
mañjuṣaka meaning "soft" in this language—
which transformed in mid-air into a precious city of vajra.
This represents the Prajñāpāramitā of ultimate reality. It is the realization of the city of Nirvāṇa, for it is indestructible. △ Second, as for the Buddhas preaching the Dharma:
within that city, the Buddha Siṃhavikrīḍita-rāja, together with the Buddhas of the ten directions, [preaches the Dharma].
This also represents the *saṃbhogakāya* and the assembly of great bodhisattvas;
according to the *Zuanyao*, these are the various great bodhisattvas from the second bhūmi upward.
He expounds the ultimate *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, it is called "ultimate" because the wondrous principle of the Middle Way is exhausted only by the Buddha;
it is likewise the foremost, supreme purity of the great cause, like a vajra. This is what is termed the "first *prajñāpāramitā*. △ 4.
The flowers form a cloud-canopy. The preceding three sections used the three kinds of *prajñā* (wisdom) to represent the cultivation of causes and the realization of the fruit;
this is the "gate of subsuming function back into essence. Now, in this present section, the three kinds of wisdom likewise represent attaining the fruit while not abandoning the cause;
this is the "gate of arising from the true to manifest the responsive."
Furthermore, immeasurable exquisite celestial flowers were scattered, which formed a jeweled cloud-canopy in the void;
this single jeweled canopy represents fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) and the realization of the true nature of suchness (tathatā-svabhāva).
It completely covers the trichiliocosm,
symbolizing the subsequent attainment wisdom that flows forth and gives rise to the wondrous wisdom of contemplative observation.
From within this flower canopy, flowers as numerous as the sands of the Ganges rain down from the sky.
This manifests the outflow of the Great Compassionate Mind, which is the Prajñā of Words. He then expounds the teachings of the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
△ Second, the King and others make vows.
At that time, King Prasenajit and the great assembly, having witnessed this event, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. With palms joined, they turned toward [the Buddha].
The Buddha then spoke these words: "I pray that all Buddhas of the past, present, and future may constantly proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā.
The phrase "in the present" refers to today.
May all sentient beings always be able to see and hear [this teaching], so that they may be exactly as I am today, without any difference.
△ Third, the Buddha’s seal of approval and exhortation to uphold it.
The Buddha said to the Great King: "As you have spoken, this Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas. All...
The Mother of Bodhisattvas:
the upper seal represents the essence of Prajñā, while the lower seal represents the function of Prajñā.
This uncommon merit is the birthplace of supernatural powers, as taught by all Buddhas; it is capable of bringing great benefit. Therefore, you all—
One should always receive and uphold [these].

The eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) and the six kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are all born from the Mother. △ Third, the Buddha manifests supernatural transformations, in two parts.
First, the general heading.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested inconceivable supernatural transformations for the great assembly.
Treading upon the previously scattered inconceivable flowers, he arose, transcending all subsequent words and thoughts regarding the retributions of the environment and its inhabitants;

this is precisely the liberation of the great sameness of karmic function. "Supernatural power" (ṛddhi) refers here to the various noble ones' supernormal knowledge of the sphere of psychic power (ṛddhiviṣaya-jñāna-abhijñā). "Transformation" (nirmāṇa)...

There are two types of transformation (*nirmāṇa*). According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: first, the power of transformative change (*pariṇāmika-abhijñā*), which refers to the act of altering and turning;

second, the power of creative manifestation (*nairmāṇika-abhijñā*), which refers to the act of conjuring up appearances. In the subsequent text, the mutual entry of the first four [elements] constitutes the transformative power of change;

the fifth, wherein the environment and its inhabitants manifest within one another, constitutes the creative power of manifestation. △ Second, the individual listing of the five: first, various flowers.
Mutual entry:
one flower enters immeasurable flowers, and immeasurable flowers enter one flower.
Within this, there is only the first entering the immeasurable and the immeasurable entering the one; these are the first and second phrases. If...
Taking one character from the preceding phrase and matching it with one character from the subsequent phrase constitutes the third phrase: "one flower entering one flower.

Furthermore, taking "immeasurable" from the preceding phrase and matching it with "immeasurable" from the subsequent phrase constitutes the fourth phrase: "immeasurable flowers entering immeasurable flowers.
The following sections follow this principle, all forming four phrases; reflect upon this. △ Second, the mutual interpenetration of Buddha-lands.
A single buddha-field enters into immeasurable buddha-fields; immeasurable buddha-fields enter into a single buddha-field.
If one considers the buddha-fields spoken of by the various Buddhas, there are both pure and defiled ones. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"The dilapidated house of the triple world belongs to a single person. It is also like the case of Vimalakīrti, where Śāriputra saw hills, mounds, pits, and ravines, yet the Buddha said:
"My land is pure, yet you do not see it. The Great Commentary states:

"Those who perceive the Sahā world do so in contrast to the Flower Treasury World (Huazang), while those who perceive the Flower Treasury World do so in contrast to the Sahā world. That [explanation] concerns the freedom of manifestation and concealment regarding purity and defilement;
here, we clarify that the one and the many are entirely mutually inclusive. △ Third, the mutual inclusion of lands within particles of dust.
A single atom-realm enters into immeasurable atom-realms; immeasurable atom-realms enter into a single atom-realm.
This means that the realm within a single minute atom enters into the realms within immeasurable minute atoms. Thus, a verse from the Great Sūtra says:
"Within every atom, immeasurable realms are fully manifested, pure and vast like space; so it is within all atoms."

The lands that appear are all due to the power of original vows and spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi*). The first half-verse explains the preceding line, while the second half explains the subsequent line.
It further states: "Within every single atom of the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*), one perceives the entire Dharma-realm;
jewel-radiance manifests Buddhas gathering like clouds—this is the Tathāgata’s mastery over his buddha-field, manifesting inconceivable marks of virtue."
This is merely for deliberation. △ Fourth, the mutual interpenetration of the vast and the minute:
immeasurable great oceans enter into a single pore; immeasurable Mount Sumerus enter into a mustard seed.
In this context, these two lines merely clarify the inclusion of the many within the one; by analogy, there is also the inclusion of the one within the many.

To present them fully now, they constitute four permutations: namely, immeasurable great oceans entering a single pore, a single pore entering immeasurable great oceans, immeasurable Mount Sumerus entering a single mustard seed, and a single mustard seed entering immeasurable Mount Sumerus.
In the *Vimalakīrti*, Nāgārjuna points to the "inconceivable smallness" where a single hair swallows the vast ocean and a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru;

this refers to liberation through karmic function (*karma-prayoga*). In the *Avataṃsaka*, he points to the "inconceivable greatness" where a single atom contains the entire Dharma-realm, its magnitude equaling empty space;
this refers to liberation through the marks of excellence (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*). Yet, in neither case is the relative size of Mount Sumeru and the mustard seed destroyed.
It also possesses the marks of virtue and liberation, as explained in the Great Commentary regarding Sudhana’s praise of Maitreya’s pavilion.
△ Fifth, the mutual interpenetration of ordinary beings and sages has three parts. First, the explanation of the primary retribution body.
The body of a single Buddha enters the bodies of immeasurable sentient beings; the bodies of immeasurable sentient beings enter the body of a single Buddha. The Patriarch Guifeng said:

"The birth [of the Buddha] and [the state of] sentient beings penetrate each other; the pure and the defiled are interfused. This is precisely the Dharma-realm of non-obstruction between phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*).
△ Second, manifesting the land of the environment (*yibao tu*).
The large manifests as small, and the small manifests as large; the pure manifests as defiled, and the defiled manifests as pure.
Manifesting as large and manifesting as small refers to the *nirmāṇa-kṣetra* (transformation land). Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"If it is the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), it relies upon the *nirmāṇa-kṣetra*, whether pure or defiled, large or small, changing and shifting from one state to another. The Buddha’s *nirmāṇakāya* relies upon this."

And they abide there. The dimensions of the bodies upon which they rely likewise have no fixed limit. However, that treatise speaks of manifesting transformations as Buddha-lands to mature sentient beings who have not yet attained the stages (*bhūmi*).
Since it says they manifest transformations as Buddha-lands that shift and change from one moment to the next, this is identical to the present text;
they merely appear again in various sizes, pure or impure. Or, [it may refer to] those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upwards, who stir the great ocean to form [a land].
Ghee and curd; transforming the great earth into gold; taking the defiled as pure and the pure as defiled; exercising sovereign mastery over the transformation of living beings;
such that this environment (the *niśraya-vipāka*) manifests as impure again after being pure, and manifests as pure again after being impure;

and as for the body of the primary retribution (*sambhoga-vipāka*), it manifests as small again after being large, and manifests as large again after being small. If one relies on this principle, the meaning is roughly consistent. Yet, how can it be that [this] contradicts...?

Regarding Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), do both the Mahayana and Hinayana schools consider it to belong exclusively to the environment of dependent retribution? △ Second, the dual conclusion regarding the environment and the body:
"The Buddha-body is inconceivable; the bodies of sentient beings are inconceivable; even the world-systems are inconceivable."
Please examine the concluding text and correspond it with the sequence above. △ Fourth, the assembly beholds and attains benefit:
At the time when the Buddha manifested this supernatural transformation, ten thousand women manifested the transformation of their female bodies and attained the samādhi of supernatural powers.
They attained the power of spiritual penetration; furthermore, they realized the Samādhi of Illusion-like Nature.
Immeasurable devas and humans attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
If one relies on the benefits obtained by the assembly when the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Practice" was heard, immeasurable multitudes of devas and humans attained [the same].

Regarding the "Patience of Submission" (*kṣānti*) and so forth: upon hearing the "Chapter on Protecting the Nation," immeasurable and incalculable devas of the desire and form realms attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Now that they have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, this too is an increase in the Path through hearing the Dharma, progressing from the shallow toward the profound.
Immeasurable asuras and others have accomplished the bodhisattva path.

Previously, when they heard the "Chapter on Protecting the Nation," the eight classes of asuras attained rebirth in the heavens. Now, regarding the phrase "accomplishing the bodhisattva path," it applies to both the stages prior to the bhūmis (*bhūmi-pūrva*) and those upon the bhūmis (*bhūmy-uttara*).
To say that they have now accomplished the bodhisattva path means that they have ascended from a lower level to a higher one—that is, they are bodhisattvas prior to the bhūmis.
Furthermore,
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges manifested their bodies as Buddhas.

Having previously heard the "Chapter on the Conduct of Bodhisattvas," immeasurable Bodhisattvas attained the stage of being "born one more life away from Buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*), which is the state of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

Now, manifesting his body, he has attained Buddhahood and immediately ascended to Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Some may ask: "Upon hearing the 'Chapter on the Third Bodhisattva Practice,' one attains the Equal Enlightenment of the Stage of Rebirth;
why then do there exist immeasurable bodhisattvas in the sutra who, upon hearing the 'Chapter on the Second Truths,' [attain this]?"

"Is it only those who have attained the tenth stage [of Bodhisattvahood]? Answer: "Among the assembly that has realized the Way, there are those who were present from the beginning and thus hear the Dharma and increase their realization.
There are also those who arrive later, who through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, may dwell in the tenth stage.

As ancient sages have also said, 'There are those with the capacity for sudden entry'—is this not an example of that? △ Part Three: The Chapter on Upholding. This extensively explains the preceding two [chapters].
[The Chapter on Upholding]. Regarding the initial intent of the seventh chapter, "Upholding," there are two points.
First, the extensive internal protection; that is to say, the thirteen Dharma-preachers of this chapter rely upon and establish [the teaching].

[The chapter] "Establishment" follows next because it extensively elaborates upon the thirteen stages of patience (*kṣānti*) from the previous "Bodhisattva Practices" chapter, clarifying realization and understanding, and expounding the teachings of Prajñā.

Second, it extensively elaborates upon external protection; this chapter elucidates the Bodhisattvas of the five directions, expounds the secret Prajñā, and eternally eliminates the seven calamities, thereby extensively elaborating upon the previous "Protecting the State" chapter. When one hundred Dharma masters lecture on it, it reveals and clarifies Prajñā.
If one eliminates all obstacles, they will come next. Second, the explanation of the title: "To receive and uphold" (*fǎngchí*) means to reverently receive the holy teachings;
it also implies receiving, upholding, explaining, and reciting them according to the rules for maintaining objects and understanding their meaning. △ Third, the exegesis of the sutra, in four parts:
first, seeing the Buddha preach the teaching.
At that time, King Prasenajit beheld the Buddha’s supernatural transformations;
stepping forward,
he saw the Tathāgata Universal Radiance upon the thousand-petaled lotus pedestal.
The *Xianxiu Fanwang Shu* states that in the Sanskrit original it is *Vairocana*, which in this [Chinese] language means "Universal Illumination.
However, there are two meanings to "illumination": first, internally, using the light of wisdom to illuminate the true *dharmadhātu*; this refers to the meaning of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
Second, externally, using the light of the body to illuminate those with great capacity; this refers to the meaning of other-enjoyment (*parasaṃbhogakāya*). As for the term "Tathāgata," it is also...
The text of the commentary states: "Seated upon the lotus pedestal, he is the true body attaining Buddhahood.
Upon the thousand petals of the flower are the thousand transformation bodies of the Buddha.
This is identical to what the commentary says: "Those thousand Śākyamunis upon the thousand flowers constitute the thousand [emanations] of Maheśvara."
Above each [petal], there is one Śākyamuni.
Within the thousand flower petals are immeasurable Buddhas;
as the commentary states: "Each of these thousand Śākyamunis further manifests ten billion Śākyamunis. Therefore, there are...
There are hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis; therefore, it is said that there are "immeasurable Buddhas.

The preceding commentary all explains the verses from that sutra beginning with, "I, now as Vairocana, sit upon the lotus pedestal," and so forth. Since their meaning is largely the same, I have cited and explained them here only briefly.
Each [text] speaks of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
However, the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* explains the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts, which primarily speak of the *śīlapāramitā* (precept-perfection) of the bodhisattva.
That this present sutra speaks of the bodhisattva’s *prajñā* is because, according to the ultimate teaching, all six perfections mutually encompass one another, just as in the case of Maitreya.
The verse of praise states: "The meaning of *dāna* (generosity) encompasses six aspects: material gifts (*āmiṣa-dāna*), fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*), and the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*).
Since even that single *dāna-pāramitā* still encompasses the remaining five, when we now speak of *prajñā*, does it not likewise encompass the preceding five perfections?
Therefore, the *Zuanyao* says: 'Among the ten thousand practices, not a single one can be lacking this [wisdom]. Thus, each is said to be the *prajñā-pāramitā*."

Maitreya. Furthermore, since King Ajātaśatru has witnessed the bodies of enjoyment for himself and others, and has heard immeasurable Buddhas each preach this sutra, he is certainly no ordinary person.
△ Second, King Ajātaśatru poses his questions.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, this immeasurable *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be cognized by consciousness,
nor can it be known by wisdom. How, then, can these sons of good family clearly understand and awaken to it within this sutra, and expound it for others?"
The intent of the question is as follows: The profound sūtras of Prajñāpāramitā are not within the cognitive range of ordinary beings, nor are they known by those of the two vehicles.
What kind of person, then, would be clear regarding principle, proficient regarding phenomena, awakened in understanding, and capable of benefiting others by expounding them for the sake of others?
△ Third, the Tathāgata’s formal response, which has three parts. First, the Dharma-preacher upholds [the teaching]. This section has three parts. First, practicing contemplation as a Dharma-preacher.
The Buddha said: "Great King, listen attentively now. From the initial cultivation of patience (*kṣānti*) up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*)."
The patience of practice refers to the bodhisattvas of the ten abodes; the diamond-like samādhi refers to the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*).
Practicing according to the Dharma through the thirteen gates of contemplation:
those prior to the stages (the three levels of worthiness) constitute cultivation based on conditions, while those of the ten sages within the stages constitute true cultivation.

All are Dharma Masters. To rely upon and establish them is to use their virtue and path to instruct people; thus they are called "Dharma Masters. To serve as a reliance for transcending the world is called "relying and supporting" (*yi-chi*).
To initiate it at the beginning is called "establishing" (*jian*); to bring it to completion at the end is called "founding" (*li*). △ Second, the command to the assembly to make offerings.
"You, the great assembly, should make offerings to him as you would to the Buddha. Present hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of celestial, wondrous incenses and flowers;

because he is one who honors the Dharma and respects people, you should thus offer worship. 3. An Extensive Enumeration of the Ranks of Worthies and Sages. First, the Three Stages of Worthies (Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat) are clarified.

It comprises thirty stages. Now, in explaining the names of these stages, I shall rely primarily on the *Great Commentary* (Dàshū) on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, while occasionally citing various other sūtras.

As for elucidating the meaning of the sūtra regarding the Three Worthies (Tri-kṣānti), I shall frequently cite the prose sections (*dīrgha-pada*) of the Great Sūtra itself; this follows the excellent precedent established by Qingliang. Upon reaching the subsequent textual passages, one must distinguish between the primary and secondary meanings.

Herein begins the first of the ten abodes, the "Stage of the Dharma Master. (Note: The phrase "法師即初" likely refers to the first stage, the *Prathama-bhūmi* or "First Abode," specifically identified as the "Dharma Master" stage within the context of the *Avataṃsaka*.)
"Virtuous one. Within this, there are three parts. First is the general heading:

'Good son, as for that Dharma-preacher, he is a Bodhisattva of the lineage of the stage of cultivation (śikṣāgotra), whether he be a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā, who practices the ten stages of conduct.'"
Initially, the Dharma Master listed the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen because they had cultivated the gates of contemplation and possessed virtuous deeds.
This is like Sudhana’s journey to the south, where he first met the Bhikṣu Meghashiri and continued on until he met the Upāsikā Śrīmati; such instances were not limited to these alone.
The *Wuxiang Dashi Ji* (Collection of the Great Master Wuxiang) states: "Those who wish to transcend the Triple World must first sever their worldly attachments."
[This is] practicing. To possess merely the body of a man while lacking the resolve of a great man (puruṣa)—Master Jing of Shibi commented:
"If one simply harbors the aspiration for world-transcendence and remains unstained by the dust of the mundane, one is then called a 'great man,' regardless of whether one is male or female.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: 'If one possesses four dharmas, one is named a great man. What are these four? First, a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)."

Second, being able to listen to the Dharma; third, contemplating its meaning; fourth, practicing according to what has been taught. Without these four dharmas, one is not called a "great man" (puruṣa).
I pray that all who possess wisdom will reflect upon this and put it into practice. II. Detailed Enumeration.
Seeing the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one gives rise to the bodhicitta;
this is the stage of the Initial Resolve (Prathamacittotpādavihāra). The *Yingluo* states: "This is a person of superior progressive roots of goodness.

Having practiced the ten levels of faith for one or two kalpas under one or two Ganges-sands of Buddhas, they have cultivated faith in the eternal abiding of the Triple Gem and given rise to [the resolve]."
The mind abides; this is called the "Abiding of the Arousing of the Mind" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*). The *Avataṃsaka* states:

"This bodhisattva beholds the Buddha, the World-Honored One, whose physical appearance is dignified and majestic, and whose marks and signs are perfect... or even hears the vast Dharma of the Tathāgata, and thereby arouses the bodhicitta.

The first stage, the Abiding of the Initial Arousing of the Mind, serves as the general [category], while the nine subsequent abidings serve as the specific [categories]. Therefore, in the preceding "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Practices" (*Bodhisattvacaryā-prakaraṇa*), it says:

This clarifies the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). It speaks only of the characteristics of the initial arousal of the mind (*prathamacittotpāda*): there are sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who perceive the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
toward all such sentient beings, they feel compassion and seek their benefit and happiness.

The second is the stage of Dwelling in the Refinement of the Ground (*bhūmi-parikarma-vihāra*). This means constantly following the mind of emptiness, becoming pure and pristine, and refining the ground of the mind so that compassion and wisdom increase in clarity;
this is called the Dwelling in the Refinement of the Ground. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "This bodhisattva, toward all sentient beings..."

One gives rise to ten kinds of mind: namely, the mind of benefit, the mind of great compassion, the mind of happiness, the mind of peaceful abiding, the mind of pity, the mind of gathering, the mind of protection, the mind of regarding others as oneself, the mind of a teacher, and the mind of a guide.

What is now referred to as "benefit, happiness, compassion, and pity" refers to these four minds among the ten: the mind of benefit, the mind of happiness, the mind of great compassion, and the mind of pity. It is also...
The remaining six [perfections] are subsumed [under this one], because the general encompasses the particular.
To personally contemplate one's own body—the six elements and the various sense faculties—as entirely impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self is the "abiding in cultivation" (*bhāvanāvihāra*).
That is to say, skillfully contemplating both emptiness and existence while increasing correct practice is called "abiding in cultivation. However...
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, this single dwelling (*vihāra*) is opened up into two gates: first, the stage of self-perfection (*svabhāga*); second, the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*).

Self-perfection refers to [the contemplation of] all things as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. Superior progress refers to observing for oneself the six elements and the various faculties of one’s own body.
Within the initial stage of self-perfection, there are ten types, namely: contemplating that all phenomena are impermanent, and that all phenomena are suffering.
All phenomena are empty. All phenomena are without self. All phenomena are without agency. All phenomena are without flavor.
All phenomena are not as they appear; this is called all phenomena being without location. All phenomena are free from conceptual discrimination.
All phenomena lack solidity or substance. The current text contains only the first four [points], yet these also encompass the latter six, as explained extensively in that commentary.
Commentary: Regarding the subsequent "superior progress," there are ten dharmas for exhortation to study. These are:

observing the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the world-realm (*lokadhātu*), the earth-element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), the water-element (*abdhātu*), the fire-element (*tejodhātu*), the wind-element (*vāyudhātu*), the desire-realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form-realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless-realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The present text mentions only six realms—namely, earth, water, fire, wind, space (*ākāśa*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—because within the formless realm, space is infinite.

Consciousness is infinite. It serves as the sixth ear. Regarding the "faculties" (*indriya*): the Qin version refers to the fourteen faculties—the five colors, the five sensations, male, female, mind, and life—as the various faculties.
These take the four great elements that constitute the body as their support; the faculties themselves are what depend upon them.
To thoroughly understand karmic actions, birth and death, and nirvana constitutes the "Abode of Noble Birth.
This means being born into the family of the Buddha-dharma; because one's lineage is noble, it is called the Abode of Noble Birth.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "This Bodhisattva is born from the holy teachings and accomplishes ten dharmas. First, never..."
First, they do not regress; second, they give rise to profound pure faith toward all Buddhas; third, they skillfully observe the Dharma; fourth, they thoroughly understand sentient beings;
fifth, lands; sixth, worlds; seventh, karmic actions; eighth, retributions; ninth, birth and death; tenth, nirvana. In the present text, there are four [points].

If one takes the two characters "thoroughly understands" (*liǎozhī*) and applies them throughout the sections on karmic actions, birth and death, and nirvana: 1. Thoroughly understanding sentient beings; 2. Thoroughly understanding lands; 3. Thoroughly understanding worlds; 4. Thoroughly understanding karmic actions, birth and death, and nirvana.
There are only three dharmas; these constitute the stage of self-perfection (*svabhāga*). Since the text does not mention further advancement, it is abbreviated.
These are the five modes of dwelling in skillful means (*pañca-upāya-saṃpanna-vihāra*), which are able to benefit oneself and others, providing nourishment, advantage, peace, and happiness.
That is to say, while maintaining the ultimate truth, one accords with worldly convention, practices immeasurable virtues, and skillfully transforms sentient beings.
Because it abides [in this way], the *Avataṃsaka* explains it by means of two gates:

namely, the ten minds of self-perfection (*svabhāva*) are the skillful means (*upāya*), and the ten minds of further advancement (*viśeṣa-gati*) are the fulfillment (*paripūri*). Thus, the Sūtra says:
"All the roots of goodness cultivated by this Bodhisattva are for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings, benefiting all sentient beings, and bringing them peace and happiness."
For the sake of all sentient beings; out of compassion for all sentient beings; to deliver and liberate all sentient beings;
to cause all sentient beings to be free from all calamities and misfortunes; to cause all sentient beings to transcend the suffering of birth and death;
to cause all sentient beings to give rise to pure faith; to cause all sentient beings to attain complete subduing and transformation. All sentient beings...
All have realized nirvāṇa. Now there are but two [remaining], namely, benefit and happiness; these consist of benefiting oneself and others respectively.
As for their further advancement, they consist of the ten [perfections] for self-benefit, as fully detailed in that sūtra.
Hearing praise or disparagement of the Buddha, his mind remains ever unmoved;
this is the sixth dwelling of the right mind. It is because he has accomplished *prajñā* (wisdom). Hearing disparagement or praise of the Triple Gem, his right mindfulness remains unmoved.
Therefore, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "When this bodhisattva hears ten kinds of teachings, his mind is settled and unmoved. They are as follows:"
Whether hearing praise or disparagement of the Buddha, their mind remains fixed and unmoving within the Buddha-dharma.
Whether hearing praise or disparagement of the Dharma; whether hearing praise or disparagement of Bodhisattvas; whether hearing praise or disparagement of the practices performed by Bodhisattvas;

whether hearing it said that sentient beings are finite or infinite; whether hearing it said that sentient beings are defiled or undefiled; or whether hearing it said that sentient beings are easy to deliver—[their mind remains fixed and unmoving].
This is difficult to fathom. Having heard it said that the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is finite or infinite; having heard it said that the dharma-realm undergoes formation and disintegration;

and having heard it said that the dharma-realm exists or does not exist—under each of the remaining nine phrases, there is the statement that "the mind remains fixed and unmoving within the Buddha-dharma.
In the present text, however, only the first [phrase] is given, as it subsumes the remaining nine.
Whether hearing that there is a Buddha or that there is no Buddha, the mind remains steadfast and does not regress;

this is the seventh stage, the Stage of Non-regression (*avinivartanīya-vihāra*). This refers to entering into non-arising and ultimate emptiness, wherein every thought-moment constantly practices emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Because calm abiding and insight are practiced in union, conditions cannot destroy it; therefore, it is called the Stage of Non-regression. Thus, the Great Sūtra says:

It is said: When this bodhisattva hears ten kinds of teachings, they remain firm and do not regress. That is to say: hearing that there is a Buddha or that there is no Buddha, their mind does not regress from the Buddha-dharma;
hearing that there is the Dharma or that there is no Dharma; hearing that there is a bodhisattva or that there is no bodhisattva;
hearing that there is the practice of a bodhisattva or that there is no practice of a bodhisattva; and hearing that there is the cultivation of renunciation by a bodhisattva practicing the path.

Their practice does not lead to liberation. They hear that there were Buddhas in the past, or that there were no Buddhas in the past; they hear that there will be Buddhas in the future, or that there will be no Buddhas in the future;
they hear that there are Buddhas in the present, or that there are no Buddhas in the present; they hear that the wisdom of a Buddha is finite, or that the wisdom of a Buddha is infinite;

they hear that the three periods of time have a single characteristic, or that the three periods of time do not have a single characteristic. In all these nine remaining phrases, there is [the presence or absence] of a Buddha.

Regarding the statement "the mind does not regress within the Dharma," the current text contains only the first [of the three] phrases; these should also be explained according to the preceding examples.
Thus, there is no error in the three types of action (trikarma), and one gives rise to the six points of harmonious respect (ṣaḍ-sāmagrī).

This is the eighth stage, the Abode of the Youthful (Kumārabhūmi). It is called the Abode of the Youthful because the mind does not give rise to perversions, nor does it incite demons or malevolent spirits to destroy the bodhisattva’s resolve.
Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "This bodhisattva abides in ten kinds of activities:
namely, no error in physical conduct, no error in verbal conduct, no error in mental conduct; taking birth according to one's will, and knowing the various [dispositions] of sentient beings."

Desire. [The Buddha] knows the various inclinations of sentient beings; knows the various elements (dhātu) of sentient beings; knows the various karmas of sentient beings; knows the formation and destruction of worlds;
possesses mastery over the supernormal power of the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda); and his conduct is unimpeded.

This sūtra mentions only the first three [knowledges] without error, because they constitute the essence of one's own practice and the transformation of others, whereas the latter seven are all for the benefit of others. Furthermore, these first three are [the results of] karma.
One gives rise to the sixfold harmony and respect (*ṣaḍ-āveṇika-sāmīcī*). That is to say: when bodily conduct is without fault, there is harmony of body and commonality of practice;
when verbal conduct is without fault, there is harmony of speech and commonality of silence; when mental conduct is without fault, there is harmony of mind and commonality of patience;

and there is harmony of view and commonality of understanding. The Qin translation states: "Cultivate the sixfold harmony and respect, which refers to the three karmas and the commonality of precepts."
Sharing the same views and studying together, they employ skillful means to discipline sentient beings;
this is the dwelling of the nine Dharma Princes. It means that by following the teachings of the Dharma King, they give rise to correct understanding and shall succeed to the rank of Buddha.

This is called the Stage of the Dharma Prince (*dharmaputravihāra*). Although this single stage is explained extensively in both the sutras and commentaries of the *Avataṃsaka*, I shall now cite only briefly from them.
The commentaries on the "self-perfected" (*svabhāva*) section explain the preceding phrase, while the commentaries on the "superior progress" (*viśeṣagamana*) section explain the subsequent phrase.

As the sutra of the self-perfected section says: "Skillfully knowing the skillful means of one's practice. The commentary explains: "Knowing the activities of the various vehicles and the dharmas into which they enter."

...and because of skillfulness. That is to say, the preceding phrase refers to skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). The *Sūtra on Supreme Progress* states: "Observing while in the presence of the Dharma King. The commentary explains:
"Entering, one observes the Father King and examines his countenance; exiting, one observes the ministers and discerns their worthiness or folly.
Likewise, when a Bodhisattva enters, he contemplates the principles of the Buddha's teaching; when he exits, he scrutinizes the capacities of sentient beings."
No. The following phrase refers to the taming of sentient beings.
Diligently studying the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) and employing supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) for transformation and benefit constitutes the tenth stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*).
This means that from the nine preceding stages, one contemplates emptiness and attains the mind of non-arising (*anutpattika-citta*), which is the most supreme.
