Therefore, the Dharma-water of all Buddhas is poured upon the crown of the heart. As the *Viniscaya-samgrahani* (or *Viniścaya-sūtra*) states:

"This Bodhisattva should diligently study the ten kinds of wisdom of all Buddhas, namely: the wisdom of the three periods of time, the wisdom of the Buddha-dharma, and the unimpeded wisdom of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)."
The wisdom that the dharma-realm is boundless; the wisdom that fills all dharma-realms; the wisdom that universally illumines all worlds;
the wisdom that sustains all worlds; the wisdom that knows all sentient beings; the wisdom that knows all phenomena; and the wisdom that knows the infinite Buddhas.
The latter phrase concerns the supernatural powers used for transformation and benefit. This refers to the praise of the supreme sutra, which says: "This bodhisattva..."
The body and bodily actions, the manifestation of supernatural powers, the accomplishment of Buddha-fields, and so forth. △ Third, the concluding section of the chapter:
the lower grade of cultivation consists of practicing the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*.

The beginning of the three stages of worthiness is termed the "lower grade. It consists of fully cultivating the various *pāramitās* as remedies for the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction (*kleśa*).
△ Second, the section on gathering faith to establish the stages has three parts. First, a general explanation of the three aggregates (*tri-skandha*).
Good son, prior to the stage of practicing patience—
that is, before the ten abodes—
one practices the ten wholesome deeds for ten thousand kalpas, during which there is both regression and progress.
The preceding section clarifies the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*); the following provides an analogy to explain it.
It is like light hair that drifts east or west with the wind;

that is to say, one who practices the ten wholesome actions of the superior grade lacks determination in their resolve as they follow the winds of either the heterodox or the orthodox. The *Great Commentary* (*Da shu*) also says: "Like hair..."
Ordinary beings on the path are unstable, drifting like the wind.
If they reach the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), they enter the assembly of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

If they reach the stage of the nature of the seeds of cultivation within the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*), their wisdom abides in principle and they attain the state of non-retrogression; thus, they enter into correctness.
This is the group of those fixed in certainty (*niyata-rāśi*). Not committing the five heinous crimes and not slandering the True Dharma distinguishes them from the group of those fixed in error;
that is, they do not become icchantikas. △ Second, cultivating contemplation to manifest the stages.
Because one knows that all the characteristics of my dharmas are entirely empty, one abides in the stage of liberation.

The former phrase describes the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), while the latter phrase reveals the stage itself. This is identical to the *Benye jing* (Original Karma Sūtra), which states: "One first enters the realm of emptiness and abides in the stage of the nature of emptiness.

The *Da shu* (Great Commentary) also says: "The *Renwang jing* does not distinguish ten stages of faith; they are subsumed within the ten stages of abiding (*daśabhūmi*). Faith is that which brings about accomplishment."
Abiding is that which is accomplished. △ Third, the conclusion on abiding and proceeding:
throughout one asaṃkhyeya kalpa, by practicing this patience, one is able to give rise to superior practices—namely, the ten kinds of superior practices of the middling noble ones.
△ Fourth, the twenty types of Dharma-preachers; first, the general heading: within this [section],...
Worthy one.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva of the nature-lineage (*gotra*) abides in non-conceptualization and cultivates the ten wisdom-observations (*prajñā-vipaśyanā*).

Abiding in non-conceptual wisdom serves as the general [foundation], while cultivating the ten wisdom-observations serves as the specific [practice]. These correspond to the "Ten Practices" (*daśa-caryā*) in the subsequent text. △
Second, the ten stages are listed individually.

Because one relinquishes wealth and life, there is first the stage of Joyful Conduct (*pramuditā-caryā*). This is called "joyful" because giving brings delight to both oneself and others; as for the phrase "relinquishing wealth and life," it refers to this.
First, external wealth; second, one's own body and life. As the sutra says: "This bodhisattva acts as a great donor;
of all things he possesses, he is able to bestow them as gifts. His mind is impartial, free from regret or stinginess.
It continues, saying that when practicing this conduct, he causes all sentient beings to feel joy and delight—this is the relinquishing of external wealth. Furthermore, it says: "He receives..."
He possesses a vast body. With the flesh of this body, he satisfies all sentient beings suffering from hunger;
even if there were but a single small creature that had not yet been satiated, he vows not to relinquish his life. The flesh of his body is inexhaustible as it is cut away;
this is the relinquishing of body and life.

Because they uphold the pure precepts, there is secondly the practice of benefiting others. This refers to the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*). They are called "benefiting" because they benefit both oneself and others. As a sutra says:
"When a bodhisattva thus upholds the pure precepts, various great Māras each bring celestial maidens, intending to come..."
It deludes the bodhisattva’s resolve for the path; therefore, one does not give rise to even a single thought of desire.

This is the precept of restraining oneself (saṃvara-śīla). Furthermore, it says: "Except for employing skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings, one does not abandon the mind of omniscience (sarvajñatā-citta).
This is the precept of benefiting sentient beings (sattvārtha-śīla). Furthermore, it says: "Having trained in this way, one distances oneself from all evil conduct through wisdom."
Entering into all Buddha-dharmas is precisely the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). The above has been explained by drawing out the underlying meaning.
Because the mind is humble, there is the third:
the practice of non-opposition (*anuvartana*). This means that patience accords with the nature of things; thus it is called "non-opposition. As the Sūtra says: "This bodhi..."
The Bodhisattva constantly cultivates the dharma of patience (*kṣānti*). Being humble and respectful, he does not harm himself, does not harm others, and does not harm both.
The first three [aspects] cultivate patience by subduing anger. Next, the [following] three subdue greed;

because they correctly accomplish the practice of patience, he does not cling to himself, does not cling to others, and does not cling to both. Finally, the last three cultivate patience by subduing ignorance.
However, the Great Sūtra fully elucidates the patience of enduring enmity and harm, the patience of accepting suffering, and the patience of discerning the Dharma.
Because these three sections are extensive, it cites only the three poisons while simultaneously explaining how patience accords with the nature of things.

Because it benefits both oneself and others, there is the fourth practice of being unyielding. This refers to diligence that is free from indolence and retreat; it is called "unyielding. As the sūtra says:
"This bodhisattva cultivates all forms of diligence, namely, the foremost diligence, the great diligence, the superior diligence," and so forth, up to...
The nature is free from the three poisons; the nature is free from arrogance; the nature is without stinginess or envy—this is the practice for one’s own benefit. Furthermore, it is said:
"By means of these practiced skillful means, the Bodhisattva causes all sentient beings in all worlds to reach ultimate, remainderless Nirvana"—this is the practice for the benefit of others.
Because there is no confusion regarding birth and death, there is the fifth:

conduct free from delusion and confusion. This means that by using wisdom to support meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is free from sinking and agitation; thus it is called "free from delusion and confusion.
As a sutra says: "This bodhisattva achieves right mindfulness; the mind is not distracted, but is firm, immovable, and vast."
Immeasurable; free from delusion; dying here and being born there with an undistracted mind; entering and emerging from the womb with an undistracted mind;
generating the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) with an undistracted mind; attending upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) with an undistracted mind.
However, the *Mūlakarma-sūtra* states that the demon of ignorance is neither disturbed nor turbid because it abides in right mindfulness; thus, it is called "free from delusive confusion.
Here, however, the term "no confusion in birth and death" is used based on a single specific sense.
Because the signless is profoundly deep, there are six "good manifestations.
This means that wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to manifest the principle of the three emptinesses; because *prajñā* manifests before one, it is called "good manifestation" (*sudarśana*).
As the Sūtra says: "The bodily karma of this bodhisattva is pure, the vocal karma is pure, and the mental karma is pure..."

Purity, up to and including non-attainment and signlessness, is profoundly deep and difficult to enter. When a bodhisattva understands all phenomena in this way, they realize that they are all profoundly deep.
Furthermore, they reflect: "If I were to understand this profound Dharma for myself alone, only I would attain liberation;
this would be a profound form of self-benefit. Then they think: "I must first transform others."
Having been born [in this state], one practices the bodhisattva conduct; first, one brings those who are not yet mature to maturity—this is the profound benefit for others.
This is because one has realized that all things are like an illusion.
Seventh is the practice of non-attachment (*asaṅga*). This is called "non-attachment" because one does not stagnate in either phenomena or principles. As the Sūtra says:

"This Bodhisattva, with a mind free from attachment, is able in every thought-moment to enter incalculable worlds (*asaṃkhyeya-loka-dhātu*) and to adorn and purify incalculable worlds, yet their mind remains unattached to any of these worlds.
The preceding citation on the adornment of lands explains non-attachment concurrently.

This is the section on the title. Next, it cites [the source] to demonstrate the profound arousal of mindfulness. This is the formal explanation of the sūtra text: "To realize that all is like an illusion," as stated in the following sūtra:
"The Bodhisattva forms this thought: 'I should contemplate the entire dharma-realm as being like an illusion; all Buddhas are like reflections.'"
The bodhisattva’s practice is like a dream; the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is like an echo; and so forth, until all dharmas are like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), which cannot be altered.
Thus, the preceding clarification that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is like an illusion shows that its essence arises from conditions;
the subsequent conclusion that all dharmas are like the limit of reality shows that phenomena are quiescent in their very occurrence.

Because they do not seek karmic retribution, they are able to practice during the eight difficult conditions; thus, their great vows are worthy of honor, and for this reason they are called "difficult to attain. As the Sūtra says:
"This bodhisattva accomplishes roots of goodness that are difficult to attain, roots of goodness that are difficult to subdue, most excellent roots of goodness, and indestructible roots of goodness."

This also first cites the cultivation and perfection of roots of goodness, while concurrently explaining the meaning of "abiding. Next, it cites the liberation of sentient beings to correctly explain the scriptural text.
It states that one does not seek karmic retribution; that sutra further says: "Regarding sentient beings, I have no partiality toward some and indifference toward others."
There is no expectation whatsoever; one does not seek even a single thread, a single hair, or a single word of praise.
The seventh preceding practice has skillful means as its essence, while this practice that is difficult to attain has the great vow as its essence.

Because they have attained the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), there are nine practices of wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-caryā*). These are called the practices of wholesome dharmas because they consist in skillful preaching of the Dharma. As the Sūtra says:
"This bodhisattva acts as a refuge for all the world—including gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and gandharvas."

"The Cool Lake" means to uphold the True Dharma and ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never interrupted. The commentary explains: "The Cool Lake" is a metaphor for the Lake Anavatapta (the Heatless Lake).
As the subsequent sutra states: "Because one has attained the *dhāraṇī* of the complete meaning, the eloquence of meaning (*artha-pratibhāna*) is inexhaustible;

because one has attained the *dhāraṇī* of awakening to the true Dharma, the eloquence of Dharma (*dharma-pratibhāna*) is inexhaustible; because one has attained the *dhāraṇī* of explaining words and phrases..."
Because she is a nun, her eloquence is inexhaustible; for she has attained the *dhāraṇī* of unobstructed gates regarding boundless phrases and inexhaustible meanings.
Her unimpeded eloquence is likewise inexhaustible—these four types of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*) are like those great lakes from which the four rivers flow forth.
He enters the ocean in continuous succession. This stage has the power of mastery (*balavaśitā*) as its essence, because in every thought-moment he manifests the spiritual power of a Buddha.
The ten true practices (*daśa-tattvacaryā*) refer to the fact that his words and deeds do not deviate from reality; thus they are called "true. As the Sūtra says: "This Bodhisattva..."
They achieve the foremost speech of truth: as they speak, so they act; as they act, so they speak.

This Bodhisattva trains in the true speech of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. In every thought-moment, they perceive unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas and their pure Buddha-lands with their adornments, manifesting the sovereign spiritual powers of the Tathāgatas throughout everywhere.
Regarding the *dharmadhātu* and the *ākāśadhātu*, the two preceding sections of the sūtra first explain the name "practice" (*caryā*) and subsequently explain the purport of the sūtra.
If one takes the *prajñāpāramitā* as its essence, then both the enjoyment of the bliss of the Dharma and the maturation of sentient beings are explained according to the capacity of practice.
To practice as one speaks is itself the truth.

△ Third, the cultivation of contemplation clarifies emptiness, serving as an antidote to the four inversions, the three unwholesome roots, the delusions and karma of the three periods of time, and the ten perversions.
The ten practices serve as the remedies, while the ten inversions are that which is to be remedied. This means that the four foundations of mindfulness remedy the four inversions such as permanence;

the three roots of goodness remedy the three inversions such as greed; and the afflictions and karma of the three periods of time remedy the inversions of outsiders regarding annihilationism and eternalism.

As explained previously through the twelve links of dependent origination, the causes and effects of the three periods are clarified: with affliction as the cause and karmic retribution as the effect.

The notions of self and person, as well as knowledge and vision, are moment by moment false and illusory. One thoroughly realizes that names, persons, and phenomena are all merely provisional designations and are ultimately unobtainable.
The former clarifies the emptiness of the person; the latter clarifies the emptiness of phenomena.
There is no mark of self or other. One abides in the contemplation of reality (*bhūta-pratyavekṣā*).

The absence of the mark of self is the cognizing mind; the absence of the mark of other is the object of cognition. When both mind and object are simultaneously extinguished, there remains only the single true emptiness;
this is called the contemplation of reality. △ Fourth, the conclusion on advancing toward practice.
During the middle stage of cultivation, one practices eighty-four thousand pāramitās for two asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
by performing these various sublime deeds, one attains the stage of kṣānti (patience).

Practicing the ten superior conducts, one advances to the stage of the Ten Dedications and receives the name "Firm Patience. △ Regarding the fourth section on the Dharma Master of the Thirty Dedications:
First, a general designation of the Superior Sages.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva of the Nature of the Path-Seeds (mārgākāra-dharmatā), dwelling within Firm Patience, contemplates the nature of all phenomena and attains non-arising and non-ceasing.
In the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) are called the "Ten Vajras," which correspond to abiding in steadfast endurance (*kṣānti*). The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"Because one thoroughly understands all phenomena and realizes the nature of quiescence, there is neither arising nor ceasing. II. A detailed enumeration of the ten stages.
The four immeasurable minds can destroy all darkness.

First is the dedication for the rescue and protection of all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of sentient beings. This means that great compassion provides universal relief, which is called "rescuing and protecting all sentient beings";
because great wisdom is unattached, it is said to be "free from the notion of sentient beings," as stated in the sutra:

The text says: "This Bodhisattva dwells in the *prajñāpāramitā*, and cultivates such immeasurable roots of goodness as great kindness (*maitrī*), great compassion (*karuṇā*), great joy (*muditā*), and great equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Ancient masters have designated this as the "substantial essence" (*tattva*) of practice.

If one follows the preceding definition—that protecting sentient beings is compassion and being free from the mark of sentient beings is wisdom—then compassion and wisdom together constitute the essence.
The subsequent sutra further states: "To act as a torch for all sentient beings, in order to shatter the darkness of all ignorance;
to act as a lamp for all sentient beings, so that they may abide in the state of ultimate purity.
The former phrase is like a person holding a torch and illuminating everything in detail; the latter phrase brings about liberation. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "It is limpid, still, and pure."
This is true liberation.
One constantly beholds all Buddhas and extensively offers worship.
Second is the indestructible dedication, which means attaining indestructible faith in the Triple Gem and so forth; by means of these roots of goodness, one...
He shall dedicate [the merit]. As the sutra says: "This bodhisattva attains indestructible faith in the Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present;
because he is able to serve all Buddhas, he attains indestructible faith in all Buddha-dharmas."
Because they have developed profound aspiration and joy, they attain indestructible faith in all bodhisattvas; because they vow to cultivate all bodhisattva roots of goodness without weariness.
The first phrase refers to the Buddha, the second to the Dharma, and the third to the Saṅgha. All of the above are drawn out according to their meaning.
This serves both to explain the name [of the stage] and, next, to cite the sutra to correctly explain the main text. The sutra further states:
"He sees immeasurable Buddhas and serves and makes offerings to them with incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewels, incalculable flowers, incalculable garlands, incalculable robes, and so forth.
Since there are extensively sixty-seven such articles of offering, it is said that he "extensively raises offerings."
Constantly learning from all Buddhas, he dwells in a mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
He dedicates equally with all Buddhas, meaning he learns the dedications performed by the Buddhas of the three periods of time; this is called "equaling all Buddhas.
As the Sūtra says: "This Bodhisattva follows and trains in accordance with the World-Honored Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
Venerable One, regarding the path of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*):

when practicing and training in this path of dedication, one perceives all forms, and even tactile objects and mental phenomena (*dharmas*), whether beautiful or ugly, without giving rise to aversion or attachment, thereby attaining mastery over the mind.

According to this passage, it is simply equal to the path of dedication of all Buddhas of the three periods; according to the subsequent scripture as well, it is equal because of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). As the text says:
Because I am likewise like all the roots of goodness practiced by the Buddhas of the past, the roots of goodness I cultivate are all identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
This is the dedication reaching all places; that is to say, the Bodhisattva causes those roots of goodness to reach all places. As...
The Sūtra says: "When this Bodhisattva cultivates all roots of goodness, he forms this thought:

'May the power of the merit of these roots of goodness reach all places—just as the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) reaches nowhere—it reaches all sentient beings, all lands, all space, and all three periods of time.'"
It reaches all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena; it reaches all languages and sounds;
it is that which can reach, and the roots of goodness cultivated are themselves what is reached. However, according to the subsequent scriptural text, whether cause or fruit, all reach everything.
They are able to extensively perform Buddha-works within samādhi.
This is the dedication of the five inexhaustible treasuries of merit; by means of such dedication, they are able to accomplish an inexhaustible treasury of merit.
As the sutra says: "These bodhisattvas possess great dignified conduct and have planted roots of goodness in the past; they enter the inconceivable..."
They possess mastery in deliberation and samādhi, and through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they are able to perform the work of a Buddha.
They radiate the light of a Buddha, universally illuminating the world without limit or end; even when born in such places, they possess such virtues and constantly perform the work of a Buddha.
Furthermore, because Bodhisattvas at this stage practice dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) directed toward inexhaustible objects, their goodness becomes inexhaustible.
The practice of the virtues of the roots results in the fruit of the ten inexhaustible treasuries; it is from these practices and their fruits that the name is derived.
He manifests various bodies and practices the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

The dedication of all roots of goodness through the equality of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). This refers to practicing virtue in accordance with principle so that phenomena and reality do not conflict, thereby entering into equality.
As the Sūtra says: "This bodhisattva may become a sovereign ruler of a great kingdom;
his majestic virtue is widely diffused and his fame resounds throughout the world. Among all enemies and adversaries, there are none who do not submit. When he issues proclamations and commands..."
Relying entirely upon the True Dharma, he travels throughout the land without obstruction wherever he goes.
Furthermore, by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), he gathers all sentient beings and acts as a Wheel-Turning King, providing for all.

In the "Original Section" of the Great Sūtra, this is called "Entering the Dedication of All Equal Roots of Goodness. Within the citation of that title, it says: "In accordance with all things, firm and solid..."
Regarding the dedication of roots of goodness, the commentary explains: "Entering" means to accord with [reality];
"equality" means firmness, because the principle of equality cannot be destroyed.
Abiding in non-discrimination, they transform and benefit sentient beings.
This is the seventh dedication, which accords with all sentient beings: that is, by means of a mind of equanimity regarding roots of goodness, they accord with and benefit sentient beings.
As the sutra says: "When this bodhisattva practices such giving, he gives rise only to the resolve to seek exclusively the path to omniscience."
The mind: the mind that relinquishes everything; the mind of compassion for sentient beings; the mind that teaches and brings them to maturity;

and the mind that causes all to dwell securely in the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). Although the scriptural passage for this stage is very extensive, these five phrases have been cited [here].
That is to say, the commentary explains this sutra by stating that the first two phrases refer to great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), while the latter three phrases refer to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

The former phrase, "abiding in non-conceptualization," corresponds to that great wisdom; the latter phrase, "transforming and benefiting sentient beings," likewise corresponds to that great compassion.

With clear and lucid wisdom, one performs profound contemplation and dedicates [the roots of goodness] toward the eight aspects of True Suchness (*tathatā*). That is to say, by uniting the roots of goodness with Suchness, they are perfected as the Suchness of dedication.
As a verse in the Great Sūtra says: "With wondrous wisdom, one constantly contemplates the ultimate, vast, and true principle, severing all states of existence."

Without exception, they are all dedicated well toward that suchness (*tathatā*). Now, within this section, first the prose is clarified, followed by the verses. In the prose, there are three kinds of dedication:
first, dedication to enlightenment (*bodhi*); second, dedication to sentient beings; and third, dedication to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The former two are practices that follow signs (*nimitta*), while the latter one is practice free from signs. Here, only [the first] is cited.
In the verse section, there is one stanza on dedication free from signs (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*). This commentary explains the sūtra by matching its parts for analysis;
the textual intent is well-supported, and it also demonstrates the skillful translation of the Tripiṭaka, rather than being the result of the commentator’s forced interpretations.
One universally cultivates all practices and vows.
This is the dedication of the ninefold liberation that is unbound and unattached. That is to say, because one is not bound by signs and does not cling to views, one acts with sovereign mastery;
therefore, it is called "liberation. As the sutra says: "With a mind liberated through non-attachment and non-binding, one accomplishes..."
Fulfill the practices and vows of Samantabhadra’s dedication; diligently cultivate the practices and vows of Samantabhadra’s faculties to attain the faculty of intelligence.

Diligently cultivate all roots of goodness, the faculty of the impartial realm of all Buddhas, and the great faculty of heroic diligence for receiving the prediction of non-retrogression from all Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, burn the commentaries on the Mahāyāna sūtras, and be fully endowed with faith, understanding, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
The five faculties. Here, I have merely cited them briefly to explain the diligent cultivation of all practices and vows.
One is able to act as a Dharma teacher and guide sentient beings.
This is the infinite dedication of entering the ten dharma realms, which means arising functionally in accordance with the nature of reality, dedicating the roots of goodness of the dharma realm.
Because they are oriented toward the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). As it is said in the sutra:
"This bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having bound his crown with a stainless silk ribbon, abides in the rank of a Dharma-master and extensively practices the gift of Dharma.
Arousing great compassion, he establishes sentient beings in the bodhicitta and acts as a guide for all sentient beings, showing them the path to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)."
The Great Commentary takes the gift of Dharma as the general category and compassion and so forth as its specific instances; all of these are the gift of Dharma.

Now, the gift of Dharma is the wondrous method for generating understanding, the root of initiating practice, the gradual stairway for entering the realm of the sages, and the bridge for crossing the sea of suffering.
An ancient worthy said: "In this sutra, the person is relied upon to propagate the Way, extolling the excellence of the Dharma Master."
Virtue. Thus, one knows that the merit of the gift of Dharma surpasses that of the gift of material wealth beyond comparison. △ Third, cultivating contemplation for receiving rebirth:
skillfully contemplate the five aggregates, the three realms, and the two truths.
This is also as in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Practice," with the only difference being that the former is extensive while this is concise.
There is no distinction between self and other; one attains the nature of reality as it is (*yathābhūtatā*).
The explanation of the meaning follows the ten practices mentioned previously.

Although one constantly cultivates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one still takes birth within the three realms (*tridhātu*). Why is this? Because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of karma and their retributive fruits have not yet been destroyed and exhausted.
First there is the thesis, next the inquiry, and finally the explanation; the meaning is explained by the words themselves, so there is no need for prolixity.
Because they are born in accordance with the Path among humans and devas:
being devas when in the heavens and humans when among men, they practice the Middle Way in accordance with their circumstances and take birth according to their retribution.
△ Fourth, the conclusion on the noble progress of the worthy ones.
In the superior grade, one practices the eighty-four thousand pāramitās over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
cultivating the two types of beneficial conduct for the sake of vast and extensive benefit, and attaining well-tamed samādhis.
All samādhis consist in the simultaneous integration of śamatha and vipaśyanā. Thus, a verse from the "Dedication Chapter" (*Pariṇāmanā-parivarta*) of the Great Sūtra states:

"Through meditative concentration, the mind is held constantly upon a single object; through wisdom, one realizes that objects are identical to samādhi. This concludes the section on the three levels of the *prthagjana* (the Three Worthies) above, and proceeds to the ten stages of the *ārya* (the Ten Sages) below.
Abiding in supreme observation, one cultivates the sphere of renunciation.
The "Dedication Chapter" (*Pariṇāmanā-parivarta*) of the Great Sūtra also says: "All have been observed; all have attained purity and vast merit."
Within the dharma of renunciation, because one is able to realize the stage of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*) of equality, one is able to realize equality;

that is, abiding in the patience of equality (*samatā-kṣānti*) at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). According to various sūtras and śāstras, it is generally said that there are three *asaṃkhyeya* [kalpas].

Regarding the statement that one attains Buddhahood after three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the *Yanyi chao* (Commentary on the Meaning) explains that Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and noble beings of the Two Vehicles, upon first seeing entry into the [first] stage, all consider it to be the ultimate. Therefore, it is said that they attain equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) after three *kalpas*.
This is also the Buddha’s teaching according to what is appropriate; thus, the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states that in reality, it requires immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Regarding *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the first chapter of the "Flower Treasury" (*Puṣpaka*) section of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* contains a commentary that provides a detailed interpretation. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there are two kinds of *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, both of which are explained in the commentaries on the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Jingyuan, who transmits the teachings of the Patriarch Xianshou in the Great Song State.

△ Twenty: The Holy Dharma Masters. According to the *Commentary on the Great Sūtra*, both the three stages of the ordinary person (*śaikṣa*) and the ten stages of the sage (*ārya*) take the bodhicitta as their essential substance.
Therefore, Qingliang [Zongmi], citing the *Awakening of Faith*, states: "There are three kinds of bodhicitta:

first, the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*), because it correctly contemplates the dharma of suchness; second, the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*), because it delights in cultivating all virtuous practices."
Third is the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), because it rescues and protects all suffering sentient beings.

That which is contemplated as *tathatā* (suchness) is also the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), for it is the wisdom of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti*). The latter two [the minds of joy and compassion] manifest the nature-virtues (*dharmatā-guṇa*) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Nevertheless, these three minds are such that when one is present, the other two are necessarily concomitant; yet among the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*), they vary in their degree of predominance. This is because, in the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), the mind of directness (*ṛju-citta*) increases. Therefore...

It is called "Understanding" (*adhimukti*), because understanding is the root of practice and vows; thus it is explained first. Because the profound mind increases in the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), they are called the "basis of practice.

Because one initiates practice based on the preceding understanding, [the ten practices are so named]. Because great compassion increases in the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), they are called the "dedication of vows.

Because the preceding understanding, practice, and vows cause all sentient beings to leave suffering and attain happiness, [the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) are established]. Regarding the three minds and so forth of the ten stages...

Because it is thus verified, it is called "well-determined. Now, since Qingliang [Zongmi] based his structural analysis of the four assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* upon the passage concerning the three minds in the *Awakening of Faith*, he consequently promoted the Great Master Maming as the first patriarch of our school;
this has been deeply accepted as authoritative by those of profound talent. Yet, those who study the Great Commentary (*Dajie*) do not understand Qingliang’s words.
I have repeatedly relied upon the virtue of the "Horse's Cry" (Aśvaghoṣa); how can my ignorance and blindness be so extreme?

Since it is known that the three minds prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) increase and diminish, I shall next explain the equal realization of the three minds on the stages. Furthermore, in each of the ten stages of this sutra, the name of the stage is listed;

these serve as proof for the five meanings: suchness (*tathatā*), the severing of hindrances, contemplative wisdom, the accomplishment of practice, and the [attainment of] fruition. Now, regarding the names of the stages and the accomplishment of practice...
The second part is largely identical in its textual structure to the verses of the previous King Puṣya.

Therefore, within these verses, I have already explained the names of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) based on the treatise by Vasubandhu, and explained the practices of the ten positions based on the meaning of the *Qingliang* commentary.

Now, I shall merely cite various treatises to explain and verify the manner in which obstacles are severed, and likewise cite the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* to explain the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). As for the conclusion of the positions:
Regarding the accomplishment of practice: where the text is concise, the sections are presented directly; where the text is elaborate, it is explained by resolving each difficulty as it arises.
Now, for the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the text has four parts. First, the initial entry into the state of sainthood (*ārya*).
Furthermore, regarding the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva of the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi), they transcend the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The Great Sūtra states: "Transcending the stage of ordinary beings. The commentary explains: "Because they have attained the supramundane noble path (*lokottara-ārya-mārga*)."
"Transcending" (*ati*) has the meaning of "passing beyond.
It means being born into the family of the Tathāgata.
The Commentary states: Just as a prince is born into a royal family, so too is the Bodhisattva. [This applies] if one is outside the teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

To leave the household life [in the past] was not sufficient to be considered superior. Now that one has attained the Dharma realized by the Buddha, it is only then that one is truly honored and supreme.

Abiding in impartial patience (*samaropa-kṣānti*) means first entering into the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*) and abiding in the principle of equality. Therefore, the following verse says: "The Bodhisattva who turns the wheel with joy."
O King. First, [the wisdom] illuminates the principle of the equality of the two truths. △ Second, realizing suchness and severing hindrances:

first, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirnimitta-jñāna*) illuminates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is the equality of the single characteristic—neither having characteristics nor being without characteristics.

The Bodhisattvas on this stage realize the *sarvatraga-tathatā* (all-pervading suchness). With non-conceptual wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*), they illuminate the principle of the two emptinesses (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).
It is neither with characteristics nor without characteristics; that is to say, this suchness is manifested by the two emptinesses, for there is not a single dharma that does not exist within it.
In the *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is termed "pervasive" (*vyāpin*), because it pervades all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
It severs all ignorance and extinguishes the craving of the three realms.

Regarding the severance of the two obstacles that arise from discrimination, these are precisely the fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), because the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) increases universally at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The extinction of craving within the three realms— this is termed the "obstruction of the nature of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*,

the "obstruction of the nature of worldlings" (*bāla-bhāva-āvaraṇa*) in the *She dasheng lun* (Treatise on the Compendium of the Mahāyāna), and the "obstruction of the self-characteristic of worldlings" (*bāla-ātma-lakṣaṇa-āvaraṇa*) in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*. Nevertheless, although the names differ across the sūtras and śāstras, their meaning is identical, as is fully detailed in the *Dashi*.
Because there will never again arise immeasurable future births and deaths.
The preceding section clarified that by severing the obstacles, the cause is extinguished; here, it is shown that by the absence of birth and death, the fruit is lost.
△ Third, the wisdom of contemplation benefits sentient beings, in two parts. First, explaining the provisional and the real in terms of the Dharma.
Great compassion is the foremost. One gives rise to the various great vows.
As the Great Sūtra states: "The Bodhisattva gives rise to such a mind, with great compassion as the foremost and wisdom as predominant.
Regarding the phrase "giving rise to the various great vows," it means that a Bodhisattva on this stage possesses ten great vows; the first is the vow of making offerings.
This continues up to the tenth vow, the vow for attaining perfect enlightenment. "Vow" (praṇidhāna) carries the meaning of aspiration. As the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"One formulates the various great vows because they follow the meaning sought by the mind."
Regarding the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), one practices immeasurable superior conducts in every thought-moment.
The preceding passage of the Great Sūtra states: "Encompassed by skillful means, sustained by the most supreme profound mind, and possessing the immeasurable powers of the Tathāgata.
These three phrases correspond respectively to the current sūtra; all constitute the study of provisional wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is neither realization nor non-realization, because one universally studies all things.
Expedient wisdom engages with existence and thus is not realization; true wisdom contemplates emptiness and thus is not non-realization. Therefore, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
This bodhisattva further exerts themselves even more diligently to cultivate all roots of goodness until they achieve perfection;
because they reverently accord with and respect the Buddha’s teachings, it is said that they "universally study everything."
It is neither abiding nor non-abiding. Because they are directed toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they do not abide in nirvāṇa due to their compassion;
because they possess wisdom, they do not abide in saṃsāra. A great sutra also says:
"This bodhisattva does not seek any material requisites for livelihood, for they seek the ground of omniscience."
They move through birth and death because they cannot be moved by Māra.
This means that among the four types of Māra, they cannot be moved by the Māra of birth and death. As stated in the previous passage:

"Because they possess wisdom, they do not abide in birth and death. Furthermore, the Great Sūtra says: "When a Bodhisattva dwells in such a Dharma, it is called dwelling in the Bodhisattva’s Joyful Stage (pramuditā-bhūmi)."
The Ground [of Joy], because it is associated with immovability;
because, being free from "I" and "mine," it is devoid of fear.
"I" and "mine" encompass the five fears, as stated in the Great Sūtra: "This bodhisattva, because he is free from the notion of self..."
He does not even love his own body, much less material wealth; therefore, he has no fear of being unable to sustain himself.
He does not seek offerings from others, but devotes himself solely to giving and bestowing upon all sentient beings; therefore, he has no fear of ill repute.
He is far removed from the view of self and possesses no notion of a self; therefore, he has no fear of death. Having realized this for himself, he knows that after death—
One is determined never to be separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; therefore, there is no fear of the evil realms.
My aspirations and joys are such that none in all the worlds can equal them, let alone surpass them; therefore, there is no fear regarding the majesty and virtue of the great assembly.
There is no distinction between self and other, because one constantly transforms sentient beings.
This means that when a bodhisattva benefits others through the wisdom of contemplation, they do not perceive a "self-aspect" as the transformer nor an "other-aspect" as the transformed.
Throughout their daily transformation of beings, they forget the duality of subject and object. Thus, the Great Sūtra says: "The Bodhisattva dwells in this Joyful Stage."
The ground. One recollects the perfection of pure mindfulness; one gives rise to joy because the Tathāgata teaches and transforms sentient beings.
Through the power of sovereign vows, one is born in all pure lands.
This refers to the seventh vow among the aforementioned ten great vows, the Vow for the Purification of Buddha-lands. Thus, the Great Sūtra states: "Furthermore, he makes a great vow:
may all lands enter into one land, and one land enter into all lands;
may immeasurable Buddha-lands be universally pure, and may immeasurable beings of wisdom fill them, according to the needs of sentient beings."
He manifests this within the mind, causing all to rejoice. △ Second, using a metaphor to demonstrate the provisional and the real:
"Good son, this initial awakening-wisdom is neither like nor wisdom; it is neither existent nor non-existent; it possesses no dual characteristics."
This refers to the true wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) manifesting in a single thought-moment. It is neither the *tathatā* that is realized nor the wisdom that realizes;
it is solely the wondrous mind, devoid of the dual characteristics of subject and object. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"When, with respect to the object of cognition, the wisdom perceives nothing at all, at that time one abides in *vijñaptimātra*, because one is free from the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper."
The wondrous function of skillful means is neither inverted nor abiding, neither moving nor still.
This refers to the wondrous function of the provisional wisdom of skillful means responding to phenomena; because it is free from attachment and views, it is neither inverted nor abiding.
The ultimate wisdom realizes the principle; because it does not seek quiescence, it is neither moving nor still. Because it is free from attachment and views, it differs from ordinary beings, yet...
He has entered tranquility, yet differs from the two vehicles;
he possesses mastery over the twofold benefit. He is neither identical to nor different from them, like water and its waves.
Real wisdom for one's own benefit is as clear and still as water; expedient wisdom for the benefit of others is as vast and expansive as waves. To draw from it, it flows everywhere.
The waters of the four seas are not one; yet to gather them and return them to a single source is not different.
So too, the arising of wisdom within the various pāramitās is neither one nor different.

Since the two benefits of *prajñā* (wisdom) are thus, the same applies to the two benefits of the remaining five perfections (*pāramitā*). △ Fourth, the conclusion on the establishment of practice through the stages:
over four *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one fulfills the cultivation of a million vows and practices.
If there is practice without aspiration, that practice will surely be solitary. If there is aspiration without practice, that aspiration will surely be empty.
When practice and aspiration support one another, they are like the two wings of a bird or the two wheels of a chariot; thus, one can soar through the air and travel great distances.
The Bodhisattvas on this stage possess no karmic habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the three realms and no longer create new karma.

Although the Bodhisattvas of the preceding ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) constantly cultivate the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they continue to take birth within the three realms because the retribution of their karmic habit-energies has not yet been exhausted.
Now, these Bodhisattvas cultivate the practice of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-caryā*) and extinguish craving for the three realms.

Therefore, there are no karmic habit-energies (*vāsanā*). According to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* Commentary, this stage not only severs that which gives rise to the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*), but also severs the various karmic fruits of the evil destinies; hence it is said that one does not create new karma.

Because they take birth through the power of their vows in accordance with their intellectual capacity, these are bodhisattvas whose wisdom is predominant; by means of their aspirational mind, they are born in pure lands.
If, however, they are those whose compassion is predominant, they remain within the three realms to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
In every thought-moment, they constantly practice the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
As the Great Sūtra states: "Among this bodhisattva’s ten perfections, the perfection of giving is predominant;
it is not that the other perfections are not practiced, but rather they are practiced according to one's strength and capacity."
Generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.
The sutra further states: "One should constantly practice great giving without end; [one should also practice] generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation."
All such actions performed are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never apart from mindfulness of the Dharma, and never apart from mindfulness of the Saṅgha;
they are vast and pure, well-established, and bring great benefit to sentient beings.
The Sūtra says: "One is able to gather in sentient beings through great giving and skillfully eliminate the defilements of their stinginess and greed.
△ Second, the Ground Free from Defilement (Vimalā-bhūmi). Part Three: First, realizing suchness and severing hindrances.
Furthermore, for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva on the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*) are the most excellent quiescence.
On this ground, one realizes the most excellent *tathatā* (suchness); that is to say, this *tathatā* possesses boundless virtues regarding all phenomena.
Because it is the most supreme, it severs the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of anger and so forth;
"and so forth" includes the habitual tendencies of misconduct. This is because this stage severs the obstacles of misconduct; that is to say, one cultivates the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
The mind severs the habitual tendencies of anger and achieves the perfection of natural morality (*dharmatā-śīla*). It severs the habitual tendencies of improper conduct.

Regarding "improper conduct," this refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) aspect within the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as well as the erroneous transgressions of the three karmas arising therefrom;
these are able to obstruct the second stage (*bhūmi*). △ Second, observing with wisdom to benefit sentient beings.
One cultivates all practices, namely, remaining far removed from killing.

The Great Sūtra states: "By nature, one is naturally far removed from all killing. The commentary (*shu*) explains that while the phrase "by nature, one is naturally far removed" refers specifically to the act of killing in the text, its meaning encompasses the [remaining] nine [precepts] below.
"One does not give what is not given, nor does one take what is not given.
The Sūtra further states: "By nature, one does not steal. The Commentary explains: "To damage another's wealth through improper means and to take what has not been given constitutes theft;
therefore, it is called 'stealing'."
The mind is free from defiled desire.

The Sūtra states: "By nature, one does not engage in sexual misconduct. The Commentary explains that what violates propriety is called "misconduct" (邪), and what involves defiled attachment is called "sexual indulgence" (淫).
The above [points] all concern the protection of the three non-virtues of the body.
One attains true speech.
A sutra states: "By nature, one does not engage in false speech. The Commentary (*Shu*) explains that to contradict one's perceptions and turn one's mind away from reality is called "false" (*wang*).
The Great Master Wuxiang said: "One who speaks according to reality is able to eliminate false speech."
One attains harmonious speech. The Sūtra says:
"By nature one does not engage in double-tongued speech. The Commentary states that this means one's words do not cause estrangement; thus it is called "abstaining from double-tongued speech.
Double-tongued speech accomplishes its purpose by being able to create division. Wuxiang said: "Harmonious speech is that which can eliminate double-tongued speech."
One attains gentle speech. The Sūtra says:
"By nature, one does not engage in harsh speech. The Commentary states that this means one's words are not coarse or vulgar; this is called being free from harsh speech.
Wuxiang said: "Gentle speech is that which can eliminate harsh speech."
One attains speech that is disciplined. The Sūtra states:
"By nature, one does not engage in frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). The Commentary explains that this refers to speech that is improper;

hence it is called "frivolous speech. It is like ornate embroidery. Wuxiang said: "Straightforward speech is able to eliminate frivolous speech. This constitutes the four [precepts] for guarding the mouth.
[This is] past.
One constantly practices the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

As the Sūtra says: "By nature one is not greedy for desires; regarding the wealth and property of others, one neither aspires nor seeks after them. The Commentary states that these are things possessed by others.
Therefore, this distinguishes [the practitioner] from oneself.
One should constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

As the Sūtra says: "By nature free from anger and resentment, one should always give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings. The Commentary explains that this means the mind does not harbor ill will.
Poison. Therefore, it is called "being free from hatred.
Abiding in an upright mind, the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, being free from false views, one abides in the right path; the mind and vision are upright. The Commentary states that this treats those of other vehicles.

[This is] seen. Because the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is contrasted with the Great [Vehicle], it is not the Right Path. This clarifies the three faults of the intention to protect and uphold [the precepts].
It is tranquil and purely wholesome, free from the defilement of breaking the precepts.
The Great Sūtra speaks of ten kinds of profound resolve that are tranquil and purely wholesome. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states:
"Possessing pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), because one is far removed from the defilements of afflictions that give rise to even subtle transgressions."
Practice the contemplation of great compassion, so that it manifests in every thought-moment.
As the Great Sūtra says: "All sentient beings mutually destroy one another;
I shall cause them to abide within unsurpassed great compassion. △ Third, concluding the stage to perfect the practice.
During five asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he fully perfected the pāramitā of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
As the sūtra states: "Among the ten pāramitās of this bodhisattva, the practice of ethical discipline is predominant."
His resolve is courageous and fierce, and he is forever free from all defilements.
A verse in *gāthā* meter says: "With courageous diligence in a single thought-moment, I shall leave that behind and abide in the true Dharma.
The above is an interpretation based on the meaning. △ Third, regarding the *Prabhākārī-bhūmi*, the Dharma Master explains it in three parts. First, realizing suchness and severing hindrances.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva on the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*) abides in non-conceptuality and, by means of non-conceptual wisdom, realizes the *tathatā* of the supreme outflow (*viśeṣa-niṣyanda*). As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"This refers to the teaching that flows forth from this *tathatā*, which is far superior to all other teachings. The *She dasheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states: "It flows forth from *tathatā* as the correct [teaching]."
The essence is wisdom. From the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) flows the subsequently attained wisdom (prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna); from the subsequently attained wisdom flows great compassion (mahākaruṇā);
and from great compassion flow the twelve divisions of the scriptures. This is because they are called the "superior outflow" (viśeṣa-niṣyanda) of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
It extinguishes the darkness of ignorance.
This stage eliminates the obstacle of dullness and insensitivity. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which causes the forgetting of what has been heard, reflected upon, and cultivated, and which obstructs the superior meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs of the third stage, as well as the extraordinary [qualities] they produce."
It surpasses the three types of wisdom. Upon entering the third stage, one is able to sever them forever. Second, regarding the observation-wisdom that benefits sentient beings:
within the patience of signlessness (*animitta-kṣānti*), one attains the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*).
That is to say, based on the superior degree of conviction and patience regarding non-arising, one gives rise to the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*):
the clear knowledge of past lives, the clear knowledge of the divine eye regarding the future, and the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows in the present.
One fully knows the three periods of time as being without coming and without going.
As the Great Sūtra says: "It is not born from the prior limit; thus there is no past. It does not go toward the posterior limit;
thus there is no future. It does not abide in the present, for when one seeks its characteristic of abiding, it cannot be found."

Regarding the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments, the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra* clarifies that bodhisattvas on these stages cultivate the four dhyānas of the form realm and the four emptinesses of the formless realm.

As for the meaning of the *Qīngliáng shù*, all its textual analyses and explanations follow Vasubandhu’s commentary; however, as that commentary and sub-commentary are vast and extensive, I shall avoid citing them here to prevent prolixity.
Non-conceptual wisdom follows in successive accordance.

A Great Sūtra states: "Because one merely accords with the Dharma, there is no defilement or attachment. The Commentary says: This demonstrates entering meditative concentration to transcend faults such as desire, so that others may emulate it.
Since this is not even the same as the self-benefit of the Two Vehicles, how could it be compared to that of ordinary beings?
Externally they were contemporaries.
Having perfected supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they attained the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

This describes how the latter arose based upon the former. Their wondrous functioning is unfathomable, hence it is called "supernormal" (*shen*); their sovereign mastery is unimpeded, hence it is called "penetration" (*tong*). — *Great Commentary* (Dàshù)
It is said: Because they dwell together with the world, they obtain only five [supernormal powers].
They possess mastery over the size of their manifested bodies and over their concealment or appearance.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "This Bodhisattva attains immeasurable supernormal powers; by means of a single body, they manifest as many bodies, and from many..."
Manifesting as a single body, appearing and disappearing at will, passing through stone walls and mountain barriers without obstruction as if through empty space.

The commentary states: this is the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhiviṣaya-abhijñā*). It is called such because both external forms and the internal body are the objects of the mind (*manas*), and because it effects various transformations;
thus it specifically receives the name "divine" (*ṛddhi*). It is also called the "basis of supernormal power" (*ṛddhipāda*), for it is accomplished by relying upon desire, effort, and contemplation.
It is also called "As One Wishes" (*yathā-icchā*), because it is accomplished according to one's will. The following four names are easy to understand.
With the pure divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), they see all realms of existence (*gati*).
As the Sūtra says: "The divine eye of this Bodhisattva is pure and surpasses that of human eyes; he sees sentient beings being born."
At the time of death, one departs according to one's karma, whether toward beautiful or ugly forms, or toward happy or miserable realms.
With the purified divine ear, one hears all sounds.
As the Sūtra says: "The divine ear is purified, surpassing that of human ears; it hears everything, whether of humans or devas, whether near or far."
There are sounds; even the sounds of mosquitoes, gnats, horseflies, and flies can all be heard.
With the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), one knows the minds of sentient beings.

As the Sūtra says: "With the knowledge of others' minds, one knows them as they truly are: whether the mind is afflicted by defilements (*kleśa*) or free from defilements, or whether it is distracted."
He knows as they truly are: the distracted mind and the non-distracted mind; the liberated mind and the unliberated mind; the surpassable mind and the unsurpassable mind.
All the above are drawn out by their meaning.
The knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) can discern immeasurable distinctions.

As the Sūtra says: "He recollects and knows the distinctions of immeasurable past lives; he recollects and knows one birth, two births, and so on, up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births, [thinking]:
'I was once in such a place, with such a name, such a clan, and such physical characteristics.'"
Such vocal sounds, with their infinite varieties, can all be recollected.

While the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that one "recollects and knows the immeasurable," the present sūtra speaks of "knowing past lives. The Great Commentary (*Dàshù*) explains: "The ability to recollect is precisely the knowledge of past lives."
△ Third, the stage of completing practice:
for six asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one practices all the pāramitās of patience (kṣānti).
A great sūtra also states: "Among the ten pāramitās, patience is practiced most extensively."
One attains great *dhāraṇī*, bringing benefit and peace.
The Bodhisattvas of this stage are able to fulfill the *dhāraṇī* of hearing the Dharma; thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"Having accomplished supreme meditative concentration and the great *dhāraṇī* of the Dharma, they are able to radiate the light of boundless, wondrous wisdom. △ Fourth: The Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
The Master’s third [section]. First, realizing suchness and severing hindrances.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva on the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī) practices compliant patience (anulomikī-kṣānti) and remains without anything to be grasped.
On this stage, one first enters *ānulomikī-kṣānti* (conformable patience) and realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) that is free from appropriation;
that is to say, this *tathatā* has no point of attachment, because it is not the basis for the grasping of self-clinging and the like.

Because it permanently severs the subtle views of self and what belongs to self, this stage eliminates the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle afflictions; that is to say, a portion of the innate aspect within the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Within the mental consciousness, the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arise spontaneously;
now, upon entering this stage, one eternally severs subtle afflictions, whereby these two views are also severed accordingly. △ Second, the wisdom of contemplation benefits sentient beings.
One cultivates the boundless factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

"Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) means awakening; "factors" (*pakṣa*) has the sense of cause, as they serve as the causes for the awakening of all vehicles. They are also called the "limbs of the path" (*mārgāṅga*);
"limb" (*aṅga*) refers to a category, because they are the causal categories for the fruit. Regarding the phrase "cultivating the boundless": according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, it is merely...
The thirty-seven factors are all-encompassing; thus, the boundless categories of the path are also contained therein.
They comprise the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the limbs of the path.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment comprise seven categories in total: first, the path that counteracts distortions, namely the four foundations of mindfulness;
second, the path that abandons all forms of indolence, namely the four right efforts; third, the path that brings forth the supernormal powers, namely the four bases of power.

Fourth is the path of skillful means for clear realization (*abhisamaya*), which refers to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). Fifth is the path of close approach to clear realization, which is the five powers (*pañcabala*).

Sixth is the path of the essential nature of contemplation, namely the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). Seventh is the path that arises subsequent to clear realization, namely the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
The two characters "fully endowed" (*samanvāgata*) apply to all seven categories mentioned above.

Because one desires to accomplish the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique Buddha-dharmas, one previously cultivates causal practices and aspires for the merit of the fruit; therefore, it is said, "desiring to accomplish. △ Third, concluding the stages to complete the practice.
Throughout seven *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he cultivated the immeasurable perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Among the ten perfections, diligence was predominant;
he remained far removed from indolence and brought universal benefit to all sentient beings.

The first phrase concerns self-benefit; the second phrase concerns benefiting others. △ Fifth, the Ground of Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*). Part Three: The Dharma Master. First, realizing suchness and severing hindrances.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva on the Ground of Difficult to Conquer, by means of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*),...

First, fearlessness regarding the dhāraṇī; second, fearlessness regarding knowledge of the faculties; third, fearlessness regarding the resolution of doubts; fourth, fearlessness regarding answering difficult questions.
These accord with the characteristics of true suchness, which is pure, equal, and without differentiation.
On this stage, one realizes the suchness that is undifferentiated in its nature; that is to say,
because this suchness is equal with respect to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa,
one abandons the tendency to seek nirvāṇa as the Lesser Vehicle does.

On this stage, one severs the obstacles to the parinirvāṇa of the inferior vehicles (hīnayāna). Now, by entering the path where the ultimate and conventional truths are without distinction, one is able to sever them.
△ Second, the wisdom of contemplation benefits sentient beings.
Accumulating all merits and fully contemplating the truths:
the former phrase refers back to the preceding factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*), while the latter phrase introduces the subsequent contemplation of the truths.
These are the Noble Truth of Suffering, and the Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path.
The two characters for "Noble Suffering" (duḥkha-ārya) permeate the three truths. Thus, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says: "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering;

this is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering; this is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering; this is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering. "Noble" (ārya) means "correct" (samyak).
This is because one has attained [the realization] within the mind by means of the untainted, correct Dharma (anāsrava-saddharma).
Regarding the conventional and the ultimate, one contemplates immeasurable truths—namely, the four truths and the two truths.
By means of wisdom, one contemplates their immeasurable characteristics, for they are examined and found to be non-false.
Therefore, a sutra says: "Suffering has immeasurable characteristics, which are not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
To benefit sentient beings, one practices various arts and crafts.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states, "Bodhisattvas on the fifth stage study the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).

The following text enumerates four sciences, which are generally explained according to the commentary of Qingliang (Xuanzang), though it is slightly abbreviated by omitting the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*).

"Letters" refers to grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), meaning the collections of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*), because they are established as the designation of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*) within the treatises on phonology. "Medical science" [refers to the science of healing].
The science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*) refers to the skillful application of prescriptions and medicines to treat various diseases.
The science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*) includes praise, song, laughter, technical skills, and incantations.

"Praise" (*praśaṃsā*) refers to manifesting virtues; "song" (*gīta*) refers to expressing one's sentiments; "incantation" (*mantra*) refers to the recitation of secret words; and "laughter" (*hasita*) refers to... [the text continues].
The entry of water into fire is called "technique" (術).

This refers to the heterodox arguments of external paths (外道), namely the science of logic (因明), which consists of: discourse (言論), conventional discourse (尚論), contentious discourse (諍論), and destructive discourse (毀論).

The divination of auspicious and inauspicious signs is also a branch of the vidyā of arts and crafts; that is to say, the craft of divination, because these auspicious and inauspicious results are induced by the causes of good and evil from previous lives.
First, there is no error.
The Great Sūtra states: "All observe well; there is not a single error. That sūtra contains passages on upholding the precepts, entering dhyāna, and so forth;
this is precisely the inner science (adhyātma-vidyā).
However, toward sentient beings, he does no harm or affliction;
that is to say, he refrains from hunting or any act that harms living beings,
and for their benefit, he reveals everything to them.
This refers to being able to initiate the practices that assist the path, gradually causing one to dwell securely in unsurpassed bodhi.

This passage, from the three phrases beginning with "merely among the masses," is identical in its entirety to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*; it differs only in that the final phrase states "non-... [omitted].
It is "supreme enlightenment. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* refers to this as the "unsurpassed Buddha-dharma"; the difference lies only in the terminology.
One knows the paths that lead out of and the obstacles within the various stages (*bhūmi*).

As the Sūtra says: "Previously one attained transcendence from the world, yet was unable to accord with the world"—this is precisely what constitutes an obstacle to the path. Now, this [stage] is able to...
To transform and guide others by means of the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) is precisely the Way of the Buddha. △ Third, concluding the stages and establishing the practice:
for eight *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one constantly cultivates samādhi and brings forth all practices.

Among the ten *pāramitās*, the *dhyāna-pāramitā* is predominant; therefore, it is said that he "constantly cultivates *samādhi*. It is not that the others are not cultivated, but they are practiced according to his capacity;
hence, it is said that he "develops all practices. △ Sixth, the Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*); the Dharma Master [explains] this in three parts.
First, the realization of Suchness and the severance of hindrances.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva in the Stage of Presence attains the superior conformative patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*) and dwells in the three gates of liberation.
That is to say, within this stage, through the superior conformative patience, they cultivate the three gates of liberation and realize the stainless, pure *tathatā*.
Therefore, the Great Sūtra says: "Within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one skillfully practices them all. It speaks of "non-existence" (*abhāva*).
Regarding "the defiled": this refers to the fact that the fundamental nature of suchness (*tathatā*) is inherently undefiled, and it cannot be said that it becomes pure only later.
It is able to exhaust the causes of accumulation and the accumulated karma of the three realms, as well as their coarse manifestations.

It is the accumulation of conditions; it is the fruit of karma. That is to say, it is the condition and the fruit of dependent origination, meaning that one is able to exhaust the causes and fruits of the twelve links of dependent origination across the three periods of time.
Regarding the phrase "the manifestation of coarse characteristics": on this stage, one abandons the obstacle of the manifestation of coarse characteristics.

This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which consists of the manifest activity of grasping at the coarse characteristics of defilement and purity. That obstacle pertains to the sixth stage.
There is no path of defilement or purity; upon entering the sixth stage, one is able to sever it forever. Second, regarding the wisdom that observes and benefits sentient beings:
with great compassion as the predominant factor, one contemplates all of saṃsāra.

Birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is precisely birth-and-extinction (*utpāda-nirodha*). Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "With great compassion as the predominant factor, one contemplates the birth and extinction of the world.
The commentary explains: "The former perishes and the latter arises; thus, defilement arises and purity perishes."
Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance.
Ignorance has the nature of delusive obscurity in initiating karma; it conceals and obscures the ultimate truth.
Karma accumulates.
The limb of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) consists of karma— namely, unwholesome karma, meritorious karma, and immovable karma— because it is the fruit arising from that ignorance.
It is the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding the link of consciousness: if it were not permeated by volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), it would ultimately never become a seed.
As for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*):
if categorized according to the stage of birth, the four aggregates are called "name" (*nāman*), while the *kalala* and subsequent stages are "form" (*rūpa*).
The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

This refers to the period after four weeks, when the faculties have reached full development: with the increase of the mental faculty, the sixth sense base, the mind-base (*manāyatana*), is established;
with the increase of form, the remaining five sense bases are established.
Contact (*sparśa*).
Contact arises from the conjunction of the three: the sense faculty (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Feeling (*vedanā*).
One discriminates the three types of sensation and experiences them through contact.
Craving for sensation without satiety is called "craving" (tṛṣṇā).
Grasping.
Not relinquishing sensual desire is called grasping.
Existence.
Craving and grasping moisten the preceding six links to constitute "existence" (bhava).
From the intermediate state (antarābhava) until the onset of decay and transformation, all are termed "birth" (jāti).
Old age and death:
the maturation of birth is old age; the decay of old age is death.
All such states arise from attachment to a self.
This includes sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. The preceding clarifies the gate of saṃsāra; the following demonstrates the contemplation of cessation.
Ignorance, karma, and their fruits are neither existent nor non-existent; they are of one mark and markless, for they are non-dual.
Since ignorance has ceased, karma and its fruits also cease. Thus, one returns to the Middle Way, which is neither existence nor non-existence;
hence it is called "one mark" and "markless," yet there is no duality. △ Third, concluding the stages to perfect the practice.
During nine asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he practiced one million samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
A great sutra further states that one hundred thousand samādhis of emptiness, one hundred thousand of signlessness, and one hundred thousand of wishlessness all manifested before him.
One attains all *prajñāpāramitā*. The *Sūtra on Boundless Radiance* states:

"One immediately attains the manifestation of *prajñāpāramitā*, which is called the light of unobstructed wisdom. This refers to the exclusive cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
△ Seventh, the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*); the Dharma Master [explains] this in three parts. First, realizing suchness and severing hindrances.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva on the Ground of Far-Going cultivates the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and realizes that phenomena are without distinction.
That is to say, within this ground, he cultivates the wisdom of non-arising and realizes the suchness (*tathatā*) of the non-differentiation of phenomena;
for he understands that the various teachings are identical to true suchness and devoid of marks.
One cuts off the subtle manifestations of the various karmic fruits.

Although Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage cultivate the contemplation of dependent origination and understand that ignorance constitutes karma and its fruit, they still cling to the notion that [phenomena] arise first and perish later;
thus, subtle characteristics continue to manifest. Therefore, within this stage, by means of exclusive mental attention (*manasikāra*), one cuts off the manifestation of these subtle characteristics.
Obstruction. △ Second, observing with wisdom to benefit sentient beings.
Abiding in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one gives rise to sublime practices.
As the Sūtra says: "Though constantly in a state of quiescent extinction, by the power of skillful means, one returns to being ablaze; yet though ablaze, one is not burned. (Commentary)
The commentary states: This single phrase alone possesses the wisdom of skillful means within emptiness and the sublime practice within existence;
though eternally quiescent, it extensively transforms sentient beings.
This refers to the practice of the simultaneous cultivation of compassion and wisdom; the upper phrase denotes wisdom, while the lower phrase denotes compassion.
It demonstrates entering the stage of the śrāvaka while constantly following the Buddha’s wisdom.
As the Sūtra says: "Although one always accords with the Buddha’s wisdom, one manifests entry into the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha. This is explained in the Commentary (*Śū*).
It is said: "Not only does he transform ordinary beings, but he also turns those of the two vehicles into the Buddha-wisdom.
